title: Budget and permit reports: housing construction slowed in 2015 (24 single-family permits) and was expected to pick up
summary: Presenting the 2016 financial plan, the city treasurer said development slowed in 2015, with about $34 million in permits and 24 single-family home permits, and budgeted for about 100 dwelling-unit permits in 2016. Later monthly permit reports were described as a good year, with commercial building strong.
status_detail: Reported for information; monthly permit reports accepted.
figures: 2015: just over $34 million permits, 24 single-family permits; 2016 estimate: 100 dwelling-unit permits, $275,000 permit fees, $769,000 capital development fees (Hrehirchuk, 2016-02-16 hearing 0:01:21). 2014 about $32 million, 2015 about $34-35 million (Warkentin, 2016-12-20 0:33:48).
notes: Dwelling-unit totals for 2016 were not reported in the transcripts.

title: 24-unit apartment project on Hanover Street approved over neighbours' objections (4-1)
summary: CASL Developments asked for a conditional use to build two 3-storey apartment buildings (24 units, possibly up to 30-32) on three house lots at 242-250 Hanover Street in the C-1 'transition zone', plus a variance removing the rule that the main floor be commercial. Neighbours objected to the height, a front parking lot, traffic, old sewer lines, taxes and property values. Council approved both, citing the transition zone and more people living downtown; Susan Penner voted against, saying 3 storeys was too high for the street.
status_detail: Conditional use carried 4-1 and the main-floor-commercial variance carried, both subject to a development agreement. Construction outcome not checked in this period's transcripts.
figures: 24 units in two 3-storey buildings, applicant asked for up to 32 (transcript 0:12:01, 0:38:57); 3 existing houses est. $600,000-700,000 assessed vs. ~$3 million for 30 units at $100,000 each (Warkentin, 0:56:33).
reasons: neighbours-object: 3 storeys too high for a mature street of character homes; dislikes parking lots facing the street (voted against). (Susan Penner); infrastructure-capacity: Answered neighbours: sewer mains are sized for expected connections and servicing is set in the development agreement. (Troy Warkentin)
public: Neighbours M.W., C.W. and J.R. (Hanover Street) raised height (prefer 2 storeys), parking lot and garbage bins facing their homes, speeding, a 60-year-old sewer line, taxes and property values. Developer C.B. (CASL Developments) said he had gone door to door, pushed the buildings 113 feet back to the park, and would build a gate to the park.
vote: 4-1 (against: Susan Penner); variance carried (moved Fehr, seconded Siemens), no dissent stated
notes: Neighbour and developer names are given as initials. Diarization splits the developer across labels D and G. The mover is not named when moving (label G at 0:57:54); identified as Zwaagstra because the chair invites 'Councillor Spijkstra' to close and Fehr refers to Zwaagstra's argument. Present: Goertzen, Siemens, Zwaagstra, Fehr, S. Penner; two were excused ('Councillor Kerrio-Penner' = Cari Penner, and 'Councillor Pincott', apparently Funk, who does not speak), so the dissent makes 4-1.

title: Lund Road land rezoned from industrial to residential and a 56-unit bare-land condo subdivision approved
summary: A 2013 application to rezone land on the Lund Road extension from M-1 light industrial to RMD residential medium density had been delayed by objections and a Municipal Board hearing. Council gave Bylaw 2015 third reading on Feb 2, 2016, then on Apr 5 approved the bare-land condominium subdivision (Fairlawn condominiums: 14 buildings, 56 units). The mayor said the units should be reasonably priced starter homes.
status_detail: Rezoning given third reading Feb 2 after Municipal Board approval; subdivision approved Apr 5 subject to city requirements.
figures: 14 buildings, 56 lots/units (transcript 2016-04-05 part 2, 0:38:20).
public: Objections at the original 2013 hearing sent the rezoning to the Municipal Board (details not in these transcripts).
mover: Bylaw 2015 3rd reading: probably Jac Siemens (transcript garbled); subdivision: Jac Siemens
seconder: Councillor Penner both times (Susan Penner on Feb 2, the only Penner present; not identified on Apr 5)
notes: No figures on prices were given. The Bylaw 2015 mover is unclear: city manager's introduction runs into 'I move this bylaw third reading' and Siemens then speaks.

title: City keeps buying Hanover Street houses for future downtown use; Siemens objects to taking starter homes off the market
summary: Under a long-standing strategy to assemble land near the T.G. Smith Centre, council bought 376 Hanover Street (Apr 5) and agreed to buy 326 Hanover Street (Nov 1), renting out the houses until the land is used. Jac Siemens voted against the April purchase, saying the city was taking starter homes off the market without a plan for the land.
status_detail: Both purchases carried; no plan for the land was presented in 2016.
figures: 376 Hanover $205,000 at appraised value (2016-04-05 part 2, 0:27:30); 326 Hanover $331,200, possession Jan 31, 2017, paid from general operating and reserve funds (2016-11-01, 0:05:36); 4 of 5 lots on that stretch city-owned after the April purchase (mayor, 0:30:24).
reasons: market-decides: Against: these are fixer-upper starter homes for first-time buyers, and there is no plan for the land. (Jac Siemens)
mover: Apr 5: Councillor Penner (not identified which); Nov 1: Michael Zwaagstra
seconder: Apr 5: Michael Zwaagstra; Nov 1: Councillor Penner (not identified which)
vote: Apr 5 carried, Siemens stated he would vote against (count not recorded); Nov 1 carried
notes: Included because it affects downtown housing stock; the land's future use was not stated.

title: Council relaxes city servicing standard (open ditches instead of curb and gutter) for a private commercial subdivision
summary: The developer of the 'Steinbach North' C-3 commercial subdivision on PTH 12 asked to switch from an approved bare-land condo to a regular subdivision with city-spec gravity sewer, piped water and 32-foot concrete streets but swale (ditch) drainage instead of curb and gutter. After a withdrawn motion on Apr 5, council approved it as a one-time exception through the development agreement on May 3. Zwaagstra and the city manager warned it set a precedent for all developers.
status_detail: Approved May 3 as a one-time exception in the development agreement; administration had advised against changing the specification.
figures: City construction specification manual about 150 pages (Warkentin, 2016-05-03 0:26:15). No cost figures given.
reasons: fairness-precedent: Voted against: approving one developer's request makes open ditches the de facto standard for C-3 land. (Michael Zwaagstra); fairness-precedent: Specifications apply to all development; other developers will expect the same treatment. (Troy Warkentin)
public: The developer's representative said the city's added condo conditions caused buyer resistance and the subdivision needed affordably priced lots.
vote: carried; Zwaagstra stated he would vote against (count not recorded)
notes: This is commercial (C-3) land, not housing; included only because it is the period's main debate on who sets and pays for subdivision servicing standards, which also apply to residential development. The Deputy Mayor chaired both meetings.

title: Mayor asks staff to look at renewing the city's seniors-housing incentive program
summary: On May 17 Mayor Goertzen said seniors housing remained a problem and that a city initiative, renewed once before, had drawn applications both times. Council agreed informally that he and administration should look at renewing or adjusting it within the budget. By Oct 4 the program was still referred to as the 'old' program, which had funded only assisted-living or supportive projects confirmed by Southern Health.
status_detail: No renewed program came to council in 2016; on Oct 4 the mayor asked how a request might fit 'the old program if it was renewed'.
notes: Program details (amounts, years) were not stated in the 2016 transcripts.

title: Bridge Park land on Stonebridge Crossing rezoned for future seniors housing without a site plan (Bylaw 2067)
summary: Bridge Park, a non-profit seniors-housing provider, asked to rezone 1.6 acres beside its campus from residential low density to medium density (up to 3 storeys) so it would be ready when government funding appeared, but presented no plan. An Albert Street neighbour objected to the unknown height, 4-foot side yards and drainage. Council gave second reading on Jul 19, relying on its administrative infill policy to protect neighbours later; the objection sent the file to the Municipal Board.
status_detail: First reading Jun 21, second reading Jul 19 (carried). The objector did not attend the Municipal Board hearing; third reading carried Feb 7, 2017 (2017-02-07 transcript).
figures: 1.6 acres; RMD maximum 3 storeys / about 35 feet, side yards 4 feet (Warkentin, 2016-07-19 0:46:19).
reasons: study-first: Uneasy approving a rezoning with no plan; asked whether conditions could be added and relied on the infill policy. (Michael Zwaagstra); neighbours-object: Concerned about a 3-storey building 4 feet from neighbours; asked whether the decision could wait for a plan, then supported. (John Fehr)
public: D.W. (Albert Street, backs onto the site) objected: no plan, possible 35-foot building close to his yard, traffic on Albert Street and spring flooding; he said he was not against seniors housing. A Bridge Park representative said they wanted the land ready for government funding and had contacted 5 of 8 neighbours.
mover: 1st reading: Cari Penner; 2nd reading: Michael Zwaagstra
seconder: 1st reading: Jac Siemens; 2nd reading: a Councillor Penner (not identified which)
notes: Both Councillors Penner spoke in support on Jul 19 (labels E and I), but the transcript does not show which is which. The Bridge Park representative's name is uncertain in the transcript, so no initials are given. Fehr's question at 1:01:04 (label C) asking to delay is not quoted because the label is shared with the city manager.

title: Lexington Village phase 2 subdivision approved: 32 single-family, 3 low-density and 2 medium-density lots
summary: Goldmark Developments' phase 2 of Lexington Village, south of McKenzie Avenue in land annexed from the RM of Hanover, extended Crescentwood Drive and created Lincoln and Nicolette Avenues. Phase 1 was mostly duplexes; phase 2 added single-family lots. No objections; approved with the road openings.
status_detail: Subdivision and road openings carried; developer said there would be about 8 phases.
figures: 32 RSF, 3 RLD, 2 RMD lots (Warkentin, 1:08:27); about 8 phases planned (developer, 1:10:19).
public: No objections. The developer's representative said presales of phase 1 were good.
notes: Grouped routine subdivision; recorded as the largest residential subdivision approval in the period.

title: Stonebridge Crossing land rezoned for future seniors' housing
summary: By-Law 2067 rezoned land on Stonebridge Crossing to medium density (RMD) to allow future seniors' housing. A lone objector forced a Municipal Board referral but did not appear, so council gave third reading on Feb 7, 2017. Councillor Siemens noted council could not see what would be built; Councillor Susan Penner welcomed more affordable seniors' options in an area that already had several.
status_detail: Third reading carried Feb 7, 2017 (Mayor absent; deputy mayor chaired). No later council involvement; development goes through administrative permits and the infill policy.
figures: Second reading and public hearing were July 19, 2016 (City Manager, transcript 0:06:52).
public: One objector registered at second reading (2016) but did not attend the Municipal Board hearing, which was cancelled.
notes: Mayor Goertzen was excused; the deputy mayor chairing is not named in the transcript.

title: Lot-line subdivision at 275 3rd Street: motion to deny ties 3-3, then tabled
summary: Two neighbouring owners on 3rd Street/Fernwood Bay asked to subdivide so one could take part of the other's lot. Administration recommended denial over drainage and future utility easements; the city engineer suggested a lot-grading plan for all 6 surrounding lots. A motion to deny tied 3-3 (Siemens absent) and was defeated; Zwaagstra then moved to table it rather than risk a failed approval vote.
status_detail: Tabled to the next meeting; no later discussion found in the 2016 transcripts.
figures: Lot-grading plan suggested for 6 surrounding lots (Warkentin, 0:09:56).
reasons: infrastructure-capacity: Moved denial: drainage costs could fall on 6 neighbouring lots and utility servicing could be blocked. (Councillor Penner (not identified which)); fairness-precedent: Hard to impose grading requirements on existing neighbours; easier in new developments. (John Fehr)
public: The applicants were present but did not speak (not a public hearing).
vote: 3-3 tie, motion to deny defeated (against: Zwaagstra, Goertzen and one other not identified); then tabled (moved Zwaagstra)
notes: Not a density case (a lot-line change between two homes); included because the vote divided. Which Councillor Penner moved denial, and who cast the third vote on each side, cannot be determined from the transcript.

title: Woodhaven/Brant Street land rezoned to high density for a 61-unit, 5-storey seniors building (Bylaw 2068)
summary: The Haven Group asked to rezone 159 and 163 Woodhaven Avenue (from low density) and a unit at 90 Brant Street (from commercial) to RHD high density for about 61 units of seniors housing next to Woodhaven Manor, plus a site-width variance. A neighbour raised light, traffic and property values. Council gave second reading with conditions (6-foot perimeter fence, access off Woodhaven) and third reading the same night, and approved the variance.
status_detail: First reading Sep 6; second reading with conditions and third reading carried Oct 18; variance carried. No objections remained, so no Municipal Board referral.
figures: 61 units proposed (Warkentin, 2016-10-18 0:46:14); 5 storeys, about 53-55 ft vs. 6-storey Woodhaven Manor at just over 60 ft (applicant, 0:50:36); 1.5 parking stalls per unit (applicant, 0:56:45); site width 60 ft vs. 100 ft required (0:46:14).
public: M.H. (Woodhaven Avenue) worried about traffic, lights, loss of winter sun and property value, but welcomed seniors as neighbours. A condo corporation letter raised access across its lot; another letter asked for a fence and trees. The Haven Group representative described a planned continuum of care from independent living to personal care.
mover: 1st reading: a Councillor Penner; 2nd reading: Jac Siemens; 3rd reading: not named
seconder: 1st reading: Michael Zwaagstra; 2nd reading: John Fehr; 3rd reading: a Councillor Penner
vote: carried at each reading (no dissent stated)
notes: The Haven Group representative's name is unclear in the transcript ('Mr. Drejer/Dieter'), so no initials are given. The applicant called it a 55+ building likely to house mostly people over 75.

title: Variance lets a two-phase high-density apartment complex on 3rd Street build underground parking near the lot lines
summary: Terrace on 3rd Inc. (MMP Architects) asked to reduce side yards from 20 feet to 6 feet 2 inches, only for corners of an underground parkade, for a two-phase residential complex at 310-326 3rd Street, already zoned RHD in 2015. No objections; approved.
status_detail: Variance carried.
figures: Side yard 6 ft 2 in vs. 20 ft required, underground only (Warkentin, 0:07:54).
public: No objections. The architect said the X-shaped plan was less invasive than the two 4-storey buildings shown at rezoning.
notes: Unit count not stated in the transcript.

title: Residential and non-residential capital development fees renewed to 2019 with 2.5% yearly increases
summary: Bylaw 2070 renewed the residential capital development fee schedule and Bylaw 2071 the non-residential one for 2017-2019, rising 2.5% a year. Councillors said the fees make new development pay toward sidewalks, transportation, fire services and other infrastructure, while keeping increases near inflation for affordability. First reading Oct 4, second and third readings Nov 1.
status_detail: Both bylaws carried at all readings; fee schedules run to the end of 2019.
figures: 2.5% annual increase to end of 2019 (Warkentin, 2016-10-04 0:11:07); 2016 budget estimated $769,000 in capital development fees from about 100 dwelling-unit permits (financial plan, 2016-02-16 hearing 0:01:21). Fee amounts per unit not stated in transcripts.
reasons: fees-hurt-affordability: Increase kept at about inflation so fees are not too high. (Michael Zwaagstra)
mover: Bylaw 2070: Michael Zwaagstra (1st and 2nd), Jac Siemens (3rd); Bylaw 2071: John Fehr (1st, 2nd), Earl Funk (3rd)
seconder: Bylaw 2070: a Councillor Penner (1st), Jac Siemens (2nd), a Councillor Penner (3rd); Bylaw 2071: Jac Siemens (1st), Earl Funk (2nd), Jac Siemens (3rd)
notes: Discussed earlier at the Strategic Priorities Committee (not public). Bylaw numbers 2070/2071; previous non-residential bylaw was 2045.

title: Haven Group asks for a development-fee rebate for 55+ housing; council says the old seniors program covered only supportive or assisted living
summary: The Haven Group wrote asking for a rebate of development fees for its 55+ seniors project. The city manager said the city's earlier seniors-housing grant program required a project confirmed by Southern Health as provincially approved assisted living or supportive housing, which this did not appear to be. Zwaagstra cautioned against funding regular 55+ housing. Council agreed to write back explaining the criteria and asking whether the building would include supportive or assisted living.
status_detail: Council asked the Haven Group to clarify; no reply or decision found in the 2016 transcripts.
figures: Rebate amount not stated in the transcript.
reasons: cost: City tax dollars should be targeted at personal care beds, assisted living and supportive care, where the city already contributes significantly. (Michael Zwaagstra); fairness-precedent: A grant for regular 55+ housing would open a new category; much housing in Steinbach could qualify. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: Request letter from the Haven Group (organization).
vote: consensus to reply and ask for clarification (no motion)
notes: Probably relates to the Woodhaven project rezoned Oct 18 (the letter refers to an 'expansion'), but the transcript does not say so explicitly.

title: Parking variance denied for a 22-suite apartment on Lowen Boulevard meant partly for Eden Health clients
summary: DeWalt Custom Homes asked to build 22 suites instead of the approved 15 in phase 2 at 295 Lowen Boulevard, with 26 parking stalls instead of the 36 required. The applicant said Eden Health (a Mennonite churches' mental-health program) wanted one-bedroom suites, faced a housing shortage, and few of its clients drive. Administration recommended denial; neighbours objected to street parking. Council denied it, saying 1.5 stalls per unit plus 10% visitor parking is a minimum and tenants could change.
status_detail: Motion to deny carried; the 22-suite version did not proceed. The previously approved 15-suite phase 2 was unaffected.
figures: 22 suites with 26 stalls vs. 36 required; existing 18-suite building uses 21 stalls; Eden Health has 40 applicants, 8 needing parking (applicant, 0:11:00); rule 1.5 stalls per unit plus 10% visitors (Zwaagstra, 0:22:06).
reasons: parking-rules: No long-term guarantee future tenants will need less parking; busy street already short of parking. (Michael Zwaagstra); parking-rules: Too much street parking near apartment blocks; no written long-term commitment from Eden Health. (Jac Siemens); neighbours-object: Not compatible with the surrounding neighbourhood given the approved two-phase plan. (Troy Warkentin)
public: Applicant representative L.S. described Eden Health's shortage of suitable suites. Neighbouring owners T.T., B.T. and C.N. objected to street parking and traffic on Lowen Boulevard and said their house had not sold since the first building went up (their claims about lost value and construction damage are unproven).
vote: carried (motion to deny; no dissent stated)
notes: Neighbours and the applicant's representative are given as initials; DeWalt Custom Homes and Eden Health are organizations. Which Councillors Penner asked questions (labels D, E) is not identified.

title: Six-unit building at 24 Ellis Avenue rezoned, with a fence and height limit added
summary: An owner asked to rezone 24 Ellis Ave from low density (RLD) to medium density (RMD) for a 6-unit building on a street of mostly single-family homes. A next-door neighbour (M.R.) asked for privacy screening. Council gave second reading with Councillor Zwaagstra's amendment requiring a 6-foot wood fence and a 1.5-storey height limit; one Councillor Penner said she supported the zoning but not long, narrow buildings on single-family streets and asked council to discuss infill fit.
status_detail: First reading Jan 17, 2017 (Siemens moved 'with reservation'); second reading Feb 21, 2017 with the fence/height conditions; third reading Mar 21, 2017 after the one written objector did not pursue it to the Municipal Board. The requested council discussion of infill design was not found in later 2017 transcripts.
figures: 6 units, 1.5 storeys, 6-ft fence (transcript Feb 21, 2017 0:20:27).
reasons: neighbours-object: Formalized the applicant's fence and height commitments so the neighbour's privacy concern was addressed. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: Neighbour M.R. (22 Ellis) did not object outright but asked for a full-length fence for privacy. One written objection was filed. The applicant (D.S.-T.) pointed to several existing RMD duplex and multi-unit lots on Ellis Ave.
mover: Earl Funk (second reading); Michael Zwaagstra (third reading)
notes: Which Councillor Penner seconded the Feb 21 motion and spoke at 0:21:43 is not identifiable from the transcript.

title: Growth paid partly by capital development fees, budgeted at $750,000 a year
summary: Both financial plans budgeted about $750,000 a year in capital development fees from new development (100 dwelling permits expected in 2017, 140 in 2018). Councillor Siemens said growth's costs are generally covered by the added taxes new homes bring. Extra fee revenue above budget went to reserves; staff said part of the fee pays for sidewalks in new subdivisions.
status_detail: Fees collected as budgeted; $300,000 of the 2017 surplus also moved to the capital development reserve (Mar 20, 2018). No review of fee rates was found in 2017–2018.
figures: 2017 plan: 100 dwelling permits, $250,000 permit fees, $750,000 capital development fees (financial plan hearing 2017-02-21 0:00:49). 2018 plan: 140 dwelling units, $256,000 permit fees, $750,000 capital development fees (hearing 2018-03-20 0:00:58). $300,000 surplus to capital development reserve (2018-03-20 0:29:58).
reasons: already-doing-enough: Growth's costs are generally covered by the added taxes from growth. (Jac Siemens)
vote: part of financial plans (the 2018 plan passed 4-3 on other grounds)
notes: Fee rates per unit were not stated in the transcripts or 2018 minutes.

title: 18 three-bedroom family units approved at 197–199 Brandt Street
summary: TNT Ventures Inc. asked to rezone 197–199 Brandt St from commercial (C-2) to medium density (RMD) for 18 three-bedroom units aimed at young families. The applicant said 70–80% of tenants in his La Broquerie three-bedroom units come from Steinbach because such units are scarce here. With no objections, council gave second and third reading the same night; Mayor Goertzen cited a vacancy rate 'at probably a historic low'.
status_detail: Second and third reading May 2, 2017, subject to a development agreement (access moved to Chapel Drive per the province's comment).
figures: 18 three-bedroom units (applicant, transcript 0:06:49).
public: Applicant E.T. (TNT Ventures Inc.) said three-bedroom rentals are about 20% of Steinbach's rental stock (his estimate: 80% are two-bedroom) and that tenants hope to move on to homes of $200,000 and less. No objections.
mover: John Fehr (second reading); Councillor Penner (third reading)
notes: Third-reading mover named only as 'Councillor Penner'.

title: First residential mixed-use zoning: 9-storey care home and seniors' apartments at 333 Loewen Blvd
summary: A private developer proposed a 9-storey building at 333 Loewen Blvd with 56 personal-care beds, 56 supportive-living units and 33 seniors' apartments. Council rezoned it from regional commercial (C-4) to residential mixed use (RMX), the first use of that zone, and approved a 120-ft height variance (RMX allows 85 ft). Neighbours objected mainly to height and traffic; the last objector withdrew.
status_detail: First reading Jun 6 (Siemens); public hearing and second reading Jul 18 (R17-141, Zwaagstra/S. Penner, unanimous); third reading and height variance V-2017-13 approved Aug 15, 2017. Whether the project was built (it depended on provincial care-bed funding) was not checked.
figures: 56 personal-care beds, 56 supportive living, 33 apartments; 120 ft vs 85 ft RMX limit (transcript Jul 18 0:34:39; Aug 15 0:25:52). Developer: a care bed costs $450,000 (Jul 18 0:40:57).
public: Several neighbours objected to the height and to traffic and sidewalk safety on Albert Street; one written objection to the rezoning, later withdrawn. Councillors said objectors withdrew once they had more information.
decision_source: minutes 2017-07-18; third reading/variance from transcript Aug 15
notes: Outcome of the building itself not verified.

title: Record 229 new dwellings in 2017, an average year in 2018
summary: Building-permit reports showed 2017 was a 'banner year' with 229 dwelling units started by the end of November, and developers created just over 100 new residential lots in 2017. By the end of October 2018 there were 126 units, 'a good average year'.
status_detail: Information reports accepted monthly.
figures: 229 dwelling units to end of Nov 2017 (2017-12-19 0:21:39); just over 100 new lots in 2017 (2018-02-06 0:04:58); 126 units to end of Oct 2018 (2018-11-20 0:14:57).

title: Townhouses behind a Main Street commercial building approved (486 Main)
summary: An applicant re-applied for a conditional use and variance to build a 2-storey 8-plex and 5-plex of townhouses behind a commercial building at 486 Main St (C-2 commercial zone). A 2013 approval had lapsed when a building boom left new apartments empty. Council approved both, with the development agreement to require the commercial phase before later phases; a councillor recalled an earlier Main St apartment whose promised commercial space was never built.
status_detail: Conditional use CU-2017-07 and variance V-2017-16 approved Sep 5, 2017; extended 12 months on Oct 2, 2018 (R18-225, Fehr/Siemens, unanimous) to Oct 2, 2019, suggesting construction had not started by then.
figures: 8-plex + 5-plex townhouses (City Manager, transcript 0:06:51).
public: Applicant D.S. said the 2013 plan was shelved because 'the supply was greater than the demand' after many apartments went up that year. Neighbours asked about traffic and sidewalk safety; the applicant had met with neighbours.
notes: Whether the townhouses were later built was not checked.

title: Narrow-lot rezoning at 209 Stonebridge Crossing sent to public hearing
summary: Council gave first reading to rezone 209 Stonebridge Crossing from RLD to RMD although the lot is 60 ft wide against a 75-ft RMD minimum. Councillors Siemens and Zwaagstra said first reading simply lets the public be heard.
status_detail: Public hearing was set for Oct 17, 2017, but that meeting's video was not transcribed (download failure) and there are no 2017 minutes, so the outcome is not known from our sources.
figures: 60-ft lot vs 75-ft RMD minimum (transcript 0:25:44).
notes: Oct 17, 2017 meeting not available; outcome unverified.

title: Council keeps a Brandt Street residential block residential, refusing a commercial redesignation
summary: Envision (Association for Community Living) wanted to move its office into 80 Brandt St, which required changing the Official Community Plan from residential to commercial. Many neighbours objected that it would open the whole block to commercial uses. Council praised Envision but unanimously denied the plan change, saying land use for the area should be reviewed as a whole in the 2018 plan review, not one lot at a time.
status_detail: OCP amendment By-Law 2087 denied Dec 5, 2017; the related rezoning By-Law 2088 hearing was therefore not held.
reasons: neighbours-object: Reasons for keeping the area residential still exist, as heard from the neighbourhood. (Chris Goertzen); study-first: Wait for the 2018 community plan review and look at the whole area, not a single property. (Jac Siemens)
public: Several residents of Brandt St, Autumnwood and nearby streets objected (traffic at Brandt/Woodhaven, fear the block would 'tumble' to commercial, property values); some speakers supported Envision. Not a housing project, but it shows how council protected an established residential block.
notes: Included because it concerns land use in an established residential block; it is not a housing proposal.

title: Eden Housing describes long waitlists for subsidized one-bedroom units
summary: Eden Health Care Services presented its Steinbach housing: 48 subsidized/affordable suites at Penfield Court and Wilson Courts for people with mental-health needs. The longest waitlist is single adults needing one-bedroom units, because Manitoba Housing subsidizes only seniors and families. Eden had shelved a Steinbach building proposal to Manitoba Housing. The mayor asked about a long-term plan to build more; council took no action.
status_detail: Received as information; no city follow-up (land, money or advocacy) found in 2017–2018.
figures: 24 suites at Penfield Court + 24 at Wilson Courts; 6–10 open housing-search files at a time (delegate, transcript 0:17:46).
reasons: other-governments-fund: Building depended on Manitoba Housing proposals, which were waiting after a change in government. ((delegation))
public: B.D., program director of Eden's Housing and Supports Program: housing is short 'especially for the people that we work with, generally on social assistance'.
notes: Court names are as transcribed ('Penfeldt'/'Penfield' and 'Wilson Courts'); spelling not verified.

title: Two extra apartments at 188–190 Chapel Drive refused over parking
summary: SPA Investments Ltd. wanted to convert space in an existing multi-family building into 2 more units, leaving 52 parking stalls where 63 were required. Administration recommended denial, the applicant did not attend, and council denied it, citing street parking congestion and the 1.5-stalls-per-unit rule.
status_detail: Variance V-2017-27 denied Dec 19, 2017.
figures: 52 stalls vs 63 required; rule of 1.5 stalls per unit (transcript 0:12:47, 0:16:23).
reasons: parking-rules: Apartment residents need places to park; Chapel Drive already congested. (Michael Zwaagstra); parking-rules: A roughly 20% parking reduction is too much in a congested area. (Councillor Penner (which one not stated))
public: Two pieces of written correspondence received; no one spoke.

title: Lagoon expansion flagged as the next major growth hurdle
summary: In the City Manager's annual report, Mayor Goertzen said the next major hurdle was likely lagoon expansion. The City Manager said the 2007 expansion gave about 12–20 years of capacity.
status_detail: No lagoon study or expansion decision in 2017–2018.
figures: Last lagoon expansion 2007; 'a dozen to 20 years of capacity' (2018-02-06 0:21:43).

title: Lexington Village grows: 71 lots with single-family, duplex and medium-density zoning
summary: Goldmark Developments' Lexington Village (McKenzie Ave, on land annexed from Hanover) added phase 3: a 71-lot subdivision with single-family, low-density and medium-density lots, then a matching rezoning and a road opening for phases 3–4. Council approved every step unanimously and called it entry-level housing that was filling quickly.
status_detail: Subdivision approved Feb 20 (R18-031); rezoning By-Law 2094 first reading May 1 (R18-098), second and third June 5 (R18-122, R18-123); Windsor Drive road opening By-Law 2107 first/second Sep 18, third Oct 2 (R18-228). All unanimous, subject to development agreements.
figures: 71 residential lots (2018-02-20 0:04:58); phase 1 about 75 houses (applicant).
public: No objections.

title: First Street townhouse infill rezoned, but council split 4–3 against a shorter setback
summary: A local realtor/developer bought six old lots on First St (47–69) to build two-storey townhouses: 18 townhouses with lower-level one-bedroom suites (36 units) in phase 1. Council unanimously gave the rezoning second reading, citing downtown density, walking distance to jobs, and developer-paid sewer upgrades. But it split over a 15-ft front-yard variance: the majority kept the 25-ft standard to fit the street under the infill policy. Neighbours objected, so the rezoning went to the Municipal Board.
status_detail: Rezoning By-Law 2092: first reading Mar 6, second reading May 1 (R18-090, unanimous); Municipal Board hearing Aug 27, 2018 (R18-196 sent staff); the Board confirmed it and council gave third reading Apr 16, 2019 (R19-102). Variance V-2018-03 defeated 3–4 May 1 (R18-091) and formally denied 4–3 May 15 (R18-105).
figures: Phase 1: 18 townhouses with lower 1-bedroom suites = 36 units (applicant, 2018-05-01 0:22–0:23); about 12,000 sq ft common green space (minutes 7.6); variance 15 ft vs 25 ft (minutes).
reasons: neighbours-object: Infill should fit the whole street; keep 25 ft for trees and sidewalks (attribution medium). (Cari Penner); fairness-precedent: Keep the 25-ft infill standard for consistency as old homes turn over. (Jac Siemens); infrastructure-capacity: Bigger buildings and pavement worsen drainage and basement flooding (attribution medium). (John Fehr); study-first: No unique lot circumstance; the variance could 'usurp' the infill policy review. (Chris Goertzen)
public: T.B. and spouse (Donald Ave) objected at both First Street hearings: sewer backups, school capacity, traffic, children playing in the street; she noted an earlier First St rezoning had been turned down. Written objection from M.M. (45 First St). Applicant L.W. (realtor/developer) said there is 'a great demand for affordable rentals downtown' but 'we're not looking to do affordable, cheap real estate', and that economics require higher density.
mover: Susan Penner (rezoning and variance); John Fehr (deny variance)
vote: rezoning unanimous; variance defeated 3-4 (against: Fehr, C. Penner, Siemens, Goertzen); denial carried 4-3 (against: S. Penner, Zwaagstra, Funk)
notes: Labels for Cari Penner and John Fehr are inferred from the chair's call and the recorded vote (medium).

title: Rest Haven care-home addition approved over staff's setback concerns
summary: Rest Haven Nursing Home sought an 11.5-ft front-yard setback (25 ft required in RHD) for a personal-care addition at 185 Woodhaven Ave. Administration recommended denial because of the mostly single-family surroundings, and a neighbour objected, but council approved, saying the community had long needed the care beds.
status_detail: Variance V-2018-05 approved unanimously Apr 3, 2018 (R18-069), subject to a development agreement.
figures: 11 ft 6 in vs 25 ft setback (City Manager, 0:09:16).
public: A neighbour objected (neighbourhood character, shadows from a three-storey building). The architect presented a shadow study and said trees would be kept.

title: 16-unit building at 122–124 Brandt Street approved after Municipal Board review
summary: Owners of two older houses at 122–124 Brandt St asked to rezone them to RMD for one 16-unit building. A neighbour (T.B.) objected that the lots were narrower than the 75-ft RMD minimum and raised traffic and outdoor-space concerns. Council gave second reading unanimously, quoting the city planner that the site was surrounded by medium density; the Municipal Board approved with conditions and council gave third reading and a rear-yard variance.
status_detail: First reading May 1 (R18-099); second reading June 5 (R18-125); Municipal Board hearing Aug 8 (R18-183); third reading and variance V-2018-07 Sep 18 (R18-208, R18-209). All unanimous.
figures: 16 dwelling units; lots 67 and 68 ft wide vs 75-ft RMD minimum (objector's figures from Manitoba Assessment, 2018-06-05 0:36:04).
public: T.B. objected (lot widths, outdoor space, traffic near the Brandt/Reimer corner). The owners said the 1960s houses were tired and costly to keep up.

title: New Official Community Plan and Zoning By-law adopted after annexation
themes: density; infill; land; process; affordable-housing; secondary-suites
summary: After annexing about 2,800 acres from Hanover, council updated its Official Community Plan (By-Law 2099) and Zoning By-law (By-Law 2100), with changes mostly limited to the new lands. At the July 17 hearing residents asked how the plan defines and addresses affordability, low-income and seniors' needs, tiny homes, and 'building up, not out'. Staff said infill policies had added almost 100 units in existing neighbourhoods in under 10 years. Councillor Zwaagstra said council encourages infill but will not mandate it against neighbourhood wishes. Both were adopted unanimously.
status_detail: OCP: first reading May 15 (R18-116), second Jul 17, third Oct 16 (R18-242). Zoning: first reading Jun 5 (R18-129, with a parking-surfacing amendment passed 4-2), second Jul 17, third Oct 16 (R18-243). No new affordable-housing policy or definition was added; we found no direct answer in the transcript to the resident's question about defining affordability. The zoning by-law did not permit secondary suites in the new Development Reserve 1 and 2 areas.
figures: Annexation: 'just under 3,000 acres' (City Manager 2018-02-06); 2,795 acres (resident, 2018-10-16 0:01). Almost 100 infill units in under 10 years (planner, 2018-07-17 0:41:10). 5+ storey apartments: 5% of new dwellings 2011, 4% 2016 (resident citing the plan, 0:29:24).
reasons: neighbours-object: Must balance infill with neighbourhood wishes and people who want single-family homes; will not mandate. (Michael Zwaagstra); already-doing-enough: Steinbach's infill and density policies are among the most aggressive in rural Manitoba. (Chris Goertzen)
public: A resident asked how the plan defines affordability and addresses seniors, homeless and low-income families, and whether tiny homes could help. A farmer from the annexed area urged 'building up and not out' to save farmland. Another resident asked council to delay adoption until after the election; council declined.
vote: unanimous on adoption; surfacing amendment 4-2 (against: Goertzen, C. Penner)
decision_source: minutes; Jul 17 second readings from transcript
notes: The 'just under 3,000 acres' and 2,795-acre figures differ by source; neither re-verified against the annexation order.

title: Lot split for a second house at 404 First Street refused
summary: Owners of a rental house at 404 First St (C-1 zone) asked to split the corner lot and build a smaller house for themselves, needing a smaller lot (4,247 vs 5,500 sq ft) and an 8.1-ft rear yard (vs 25 ft). Neighbours objected. Council unanimously denied the variance and subdivision, with Councillor Siemens saying past corner-lot splits produced two homes with very small yards.
status_detail: Variance V-2018-10 (R18-135) and subdivision 4451-2018-8015 (R18-136) denied unanimously, Jun 19, 2018.
figures: 4,247 sq ft vs 5,500 minimum; 8.1-ft vs 25-ft rear yard (City Manager, 0:07:49).
reasons: neighbours-object: Many neighbours expressed concerns; the variance is permanent, not tied to the current owners. (Michael Zwaagstra); fairness-precedent: Council has denied similar lot splits elsewhere; small-yard lots on a busy corner. (Jac Siemens)
public: Owners A.H. and H.H. wanted to keep the existing house as a rental for income. Neighbours objected (drainage, privacy, a busy corner).

title: City objects to Hanover's development plan for land around Steinbach, then withdraws after changes
summary: Steinbach objected to the RM of Hanover's draft development plan, chiefly its land-use policies for the transitional area around the city (land Steinbach had failed to annex) and a proposed rural business area. After Hanover amended the plan, council withdrew the objection. The city also objected to La Broquerie's development plan and zoning by-law in August.
status_detail: Objection Jun 19 (R18-138, Zwaagstra/S. Penner, unanimous); withdrawn Oct 2 (R18-235, C. Penner/Siemens, unanimous). La Broquerie objections Aug 7 (R18-175, R18-176).

title: City buys three Hanover Street houses for future downtown development; Fehr objects
summary: Continuing a 25-year downtown land-assembly strategy, council bought 336, 332 and 380 Hanover St. Councillor Funk said the lots could later hold mixed-use or multi-family housing, raising density; Councillor Fehr voted against each purchase, saying the city was pushing residents away from downtown. The houses were to be rented out until needed.
status_detail: Purchases carried 5-1 (Jul 3, R18-152; Aug 7, R18-174) and 6-1 (Oct 16, R18-238), Fehr against each. Future use not decided in 2018.
figures: 336 Hanover $194,500; 332 Hanover $172,900; 380 Hanover $280,000 (minutes).
mover: Earl Funk; Cari Penner; Cari Penner
seconder: Michael Zwaagstra; Susan Penner; Susan Penner
notes: Mayor Goertzen was excused Jul 3; Deputy Mayor chaired.

title: Harmony Lane subdivision redesign passes 4–3 over a new homeowner's objection
summary: Prairie Homes Inc. (and a related numbered company) took over a multi-phase subdivision near Harmony Lane and asked to reconfigure lots, temporarily close and reopen part of a public reserve, and rezone lots to RSF/RLD. A new homeowner (G.D.) objected that he had bought on the promise of green-space access. Council split 4–3 on closing the reserve: the majority said fewer future variances meant better planning; Siemens, Funk and Fehr said the public hearing input should prevail. The developer later offered the objector an easement and third reading passed unanimously.
status_detail: Subdivision 4451-2018-7990 conditionally approved Jul 3 (R18-154, unanimous). By-Law 2102 second reading Oct 16, 4-3 (R18-249); rezoning By-Law 2103 second reading unanimous (R18-250). Third reading of 2102 unanimous Dec 4, 2018 (R18-279) after the developer resolved the objection; 2103 third reading Jan 15, 2019 (R19-007).
figures: 9 new lots plus 3 lots redesignated RSF→RLD (City Manager, 2018-10-16 0:01–0:13).
reasons: neighbours-object: The public hearing was residents' only chance for input; council should listen. (Jac Siemens); fairness-precedent: The homeowner did his homework and was told nothing would change. (Earl Funk)
public: G.D. (Chrysler Gate) objected that his purchase relied on 10 ft of green-space access shown in the plans. A written objection (L.R.) was received on the Jul 3 subdivision. G.D. later accepted the developer's easement offer.
vote: 4-3 on Oct 16 (against: Siemens, Funk, Fehr); unanimous otherwise

title: 44 three-bedroom townhouses on Maplewood Street refused, 5–1
summary: TNT Ventures Inc. sought to rezone seven lots at 135–191 Maplewood St from RLD to RMD for 44 three-bedroom condo-townhouses in four buildings over 4–5 years. Neighbours submitted 49 letters with 84 signatures, citing traffic, drainage and the applicant's upkeep of his existing rentals. Council denied second reading, 5–1, saying the plan was unclear and too large a change; Councillor Susan Penner alone voted to proceed.
status_detail: First reading Jul 17 (Fehr/Funk); second reading denied Aug 21, 2018 (R18-191), which ends the by-law. Several councillors said a reworked plan or duplexes could work.
figures: 44 units (4 buildings x 11), 2 parking stalls per unit vs 1.5 required (minutes 2018-08-21 item 10.5); 49 letters / 84 signatures (minutes item 10.6).
reasons: neighbours-object: A multi-lot change of this size requires listening to neighbours; plan unclear; likely to fail at the Municipal Board anyway. (Michael Zwaagstra); infrastructure-capacity: Overland drainage from more pavement, near existing Holmes St drainage problems. (Jac Siemens); neighbours-object: Lack of neighbours' trust in the developer; drainage. (Earl Funk); neighbours-object: Developer needs to make it fit and ease neighbours' concerns. (Cari Penner)
public: Many neighbours objected (traffic, drainage, privacy, schools, upkeep of the applicant's existing rental houses); one said duplexes would be acceptable. Applicant E.T. (TNT Ventures Inc.) said the houses were old, that he builds about 10 three-bedroom townhouses a year in La Broquerie, and that Morden and Winkler build multi-family into new subdivisions from the start. Claims about the applicant's property upkeep are residents' allegations, unproven.
notes: Applicant's name appears in minutes as 'Elmer Toews' and in transcript as 'Elmer Taves'; shown as E.T.

title: Duplex-zoned corner lots approved for single-family homes only
summary: Poplar Estates Ltd. asked for 5-ft side yards (8 ft required in RLD) on two Alderwood Crescent corner lots to build single-family homes, instead of rezoning the duplex-zoned lots down to single-family. Council approved on condition that only single-family dwellings be built; Councillor Fehr voted against after asking about corner-lot sidewalk room.
status_detail: Variance V-2018-22 approved 6-1 (R18-210), Fehr against.
figures: 5-ft vs 8-ft side yard (City Manager, 0:07:20).
public: One letter received; no one spoke against.
notes: Fehr's reason is inferred from his question; he did not state it.

title: New single-family and low-density subdivisions approved phase by phase (about 150+ lots)
summary: Council approved a steady stream of developer-led subdivisions, each subject to a development agreement: Goldmark's Lexington Village phases (Windsor Gate/York/Essex, 46 RLD lots, Phase 5), the Prairie Crescent/Malibu/Alpine phase (49 lots), Hampton Village's switch from RMD to single-family (Winston Place), and smaller splits. In January 2020 nine single-family lots on Windsor Gate were changed to six duplex lots and one single-family lot. Councillors said lot inventory was low and new lots met demand.
status_detail: All approved unanimously: By-Law 2103 (R19-007, Jan 15, 2019); Goldmark subdivision 8099 (R19-047, Mar 5, 2019); By-Law 2126 and subdivision 8186 (R19-190 to R19-192, Oct 1, 2019; amended to duplex lots R20-016, Jan 21, 2020); Two Knew subdivision 8174 (R19-201, Oct 15, 2019); By-Law 2141 Lexington Phase 5 (R20-035, R20-068, R20-069); By-Law 2145 and subdivision 8244 (R20-070 to R20-072, Apr 7, 2020); By-Law 2154 and subdivision 8330 (R20-150, R20-171 to R20-173); Millbrook subdivisions (R20-205, R20-206, Oct 20, 2020).
figures: 46 RLD lots (2019-10-01 transcript 0:10:28, City Manager); 49 lots: 32 RSF and 17 RLD (2020-04-07 transcript; developer said 10th phase); 9 single-family lots to 6 duplex + 1 single-family (2020-01-21 transcript 0:23:44).
public: Few objections; no one spoke against the Prairie Crescent phase (2020-04-07).
mover: various (mostly Zwaagstra, D. Penner, S. Penner)
notes: Lot counts are given only where stated in a transcript; totals are approximate.

title: After-the-fact landscaping variance for a new 16-unit apartment block denied 5-2
summary: The owners of a newly built 16-unit apartment block at 29 Cambridge Way (Gem Ventures) asked council to waive the street-edge planter with 2 trees and 9 shrubs required by the zoning by-law and their development agreement, which their builder had missed. Susan Penner and Jac Siemens wanted to approve it with the trees planted elsewhere on the site; the majority said approving an after-the-fact request would set a precedent for developers to build first and ask forgiveness later.
status_detail: Motion to approve (S. Penner/Siemens, R19-003) defeated 2-5; motion to deny (Zwaagstra/J. Hiebert, R19-004) carried 5-2. The required landscaping had to be installed.
figures: 16 units; 2 trees and 9 shrubs required; multifamily parking standard 1.5 stalls per unit plus 10%, 25 stalls required after a minor variance (transcript 0:20:41, City Manager).
reasons: fairness-precedent: Approving after construction would invite developers to build first and ask forgiveness; the landscaping standard is a good policy that council is not changing. (Michael Zwaagstra); fairness-precedent: Developers have multiple checks to follow; approving would set a bad standard for future variances. (Damian Penner (medium-confidence identification))
public: The applicants (J.U. and M.U., Gem Ventures Ltd.) said the plan they bought omitted the planter and that tearing up the finished lot would be costly; no one objected.
mover: R19-003 Susan Penner; R19-004 Michael Zwaagstra
seconder: R19-003 Jac Siemens; R19-004 Jake Hiebert
vote: R19-003 2-5 (for: S. Penner, Siemens); R19-004 5-2 (against: S. Penner, Siemens)
notes: Bill Hiebert's and Damian Penner's labels in this file are inferred from the chair's (mis-transcribed) names; their stances come from the minutes' recorded vote.

title: Council objects to rural-residential development planned just outside city limits
summary: Council formally objected to the RM of La Broquerie's development plan (March 5) and to an RM of Hanover amendment designating a quarter section just west of the city boundary as rural residential (April 2). Staff said the Hanover change conflicted with provincial land-use policy and the Steinbach-Hanover annexation agreement; councillors said it would leapfrog the city and block the sewer route needed for growth to the southwest.
status_detail: Objections authorized unanimously: La Broquerie (R19-051, Zwaagstra/S. Penner, March 5, 2019) and Hanover By-Laws 2437-19/2438-19 (R19-083, S. Penner/D. Penner, April 2, 2019). The outcome of the RMs' hearings was not found in council records.
figures: One quarter section west of the joint boundary (2019-04-02 transcript 0:18:33, City Manager).
reasons: infrastructure-capacity: Rural development leapfrogging the boundary conflicts with provincial policy on eventual connection to city services. (Susan Penner)
mover: R19-051 Michael Zwaagstra; R19-083 Susan Penner
seconder: R19-051 Susan Penner; R19-083 Damian Penner
notes: No transcript for March 5, 2019 (La Broquerie); that objection relies on minutes.

title: Housing growth reports: 1,859 units in a decade, 257 in 2020, and rental vacancy near 1%
summary: Monthly building-permit reports tracked growth: the 2019 plan expected about 140 new dwelling units; 2020 reached 257 units by the December meeting despite COVID-19, with many multifamily permits (a 45-unit building on Penfield Drive, two 12-unit buildings on Maplewood, an 18-unit building on Brighton Lane). Applicants cited CMHC vacancy rates of 1.3% (2019) and 1.2% (2019 data), and councillors said vacancy stays low however many units are approved. Council received these as information; no housing needs assessment or target was set.
status_detail: Reports received as information. No housing strategy, needs assessment or affordability target was adopted in 2019-2020.
figures: 2019 forecast 140 dwelling units (2019-03-19 transcript, budget presentation); 93 units by end of August 2019 (2019-09-17 transcript); 1,859 units added 2009-2019 (2020-01-21 transcript 0:00:17, Susan Penner); 156 units by Sept 2020 (2020-10-06); 257 units and $58.5M permits by the Dec 15, 2020 report (transcript 0:42:29); $7.1M 45-unit multiplex on Penfield Drive (2020-08-18).
notes: Unit counts are as read at meetings; the year-end 2019 total was not found (no transcripts Oct 15 - Dec 17, 2019).

title: Infill developer's $10,000-per-lot demolition grant request denied under the developer-pay policy
summary: The developer of the First Street multi-family project (L.W., through two numbered companies) asked for a $10,000-per-lot demolition grant because Municipal Board conditions had made the infill project costlier. Council unanimously refused, saying Steinbach has followed a developer-pay policy since the 1980s, taxpayers should not make up the difference, and city by-laws only allow grants to non-profits.
status_detail: Denied unanimously (R19-075). No infill or redevelopment incentive was created in this period.
figures: $10,000 per lot; about 6 lots, roughly $60,000 (transcript 0:49:56, Zwaagstra).
reasons: developer-pays: Residential development in Steinbach is developer paid; taxpayers should not cover cost increases. (Michael Zwaagstra); fairness-precedent: Every developer whose project became costlier would ask for the same; unfair to past developers who paid their own way. (Michael Zwaagstra); developer-pays: City has followed a developer-pay policy since the 1980s; no by-law allows grants to for-profit firms. (Jac Siemens); fairness-precedent: Precedent, and by-laws do not allow such a grant. (Earl Funk)
public: Request came by letter from the developer (L.W., Royal LePage; 6135367 MB Inc. and 5563985 MB Ltd.).
notes: Same item is recorded in the taxes-spending 2019-2020 file. The developer is a member of the public and is identified by initials.

title: 126 Maplewood rezoned for a 9-unit apartment despite a 56-name neighbourhood petition
summary: By-Law 2120 rezoned 126 Maplewood Street from RSF/RLD to RMD so an older rental could be replaced by a 9-unit building with bachelor and one-bedroom suites; a site-width variance (56 ft vs. 75 ft) was also needed. A neighbour presented a petition of 56 names; others raised traffic, drainage, property values and the kind of tenants, while one resident welcomed small units. Council approved unanimously, noting nearby apartments, the unusually deep lot, and that renters are not 'riffraff'.
status_detail: First reading April 16 (R19-101), second reading after the May 21 hearing (R19-118), third reading July 2, 2019 subject to a development agreement (R19-147) and site-width variance approved (R19-148); all unanimous.
figures: 9 units, mostly bachelor/one-bedroom (transcript 2019-05-21 0:08:04, applicant); site width 56 ft vs. 75 ft minimum (0:05:06, City Manager); petition of 56 names (0:10:02).
public: R.W. (184 Maplewood) presented a 56-signature petition: 'We want to keep it a family community. We do not want apartments.' Other neighbours (I.F., C.F., J.R., W.C.) cited construction, variance size, traffic, drainage and property values; A.D. spoke in favour of bachelor and one-bedroom units for young and low-income people. The applicant (H.B.) said his existing units have a waiting list.
mover: R19-101 Damian Penner; R19-118 Michael Zwaagstra; R19-147 Jac Siemens; R19-148 Michael Zwaagstra
seconder: R19-101 Michael Zwaagstra; R19-118 Jac Siemens; R19-147 Damian Penner; R19-148 Damian Penner
notes: Jake/Bill Hiebert comments in this hearing (labels J and Q) could not be told apart and are not quoted.

title: First Street (north side) rezoning for up to 64 units finally passed after a Municipal Board hearing
summary: By-Law 2092 rezoned six lots on the north side of First Street from RLD to RMD for a multi-family infill project. Objections at the May 2018 hearing sent it to the Manitoba Municipal Board, which confirmed the by-law with added conditions. In 2019 council gave third reading and approved consolidating the six lots into two multifamily lots, as the Board required.
status_detail: Third reading April 16, 2019 (R19-102, Zwaagstra/D. Penner, unanimous), subject to a development agreement that includes the Board's conditions and the city's infill policy; lot consolidation approved June 4, 2019 (resolution printed as R18-127, Zwaagstra/D. Penner). Staff said in July 2019 the two properties were being redeveloped with up to 64 dwelling units.
figures: 6 lots consolidated into 2 multifamily lots (2019-06-04 transcript 0:07:33); up to 64 dwelling units (2019-07-16 transcript, City Manager introduction of By-Law 2125).
public: Objections registered at the 2018 hearing triggered the Municipal Board review (minutes 2019-04-16). The developer (L.W.) later said the Board's extra conditions made the project costlier (see 2019-demolition-grant-developer-pay).
notes: The June 4, 2019 minutes print the resolution number as R18-127 (apparently a typo for R19-127).

title: 8-unit infill at 44 First Street approved 4-3 over neighbours' and three councillors' objections
summary: By-Law 2125 rezoned 44 First Street (south side) from RLD to RMD for an 8-unit, two-storey building with four one-bedroom and four three-bedroom suites, plus a 70-ft site-width variance. Neighbours and a nearby developer objected (setbacks, privacy, traffic, precedent). Jac Siemens, Jake Hiebert and Bill Hiebert said the community plan meant the south side to stay single-family or duplex; the majority said medium density is still 'residential' under the plan, the project met the infill policy, and one-bedroom units were badly needed.
status_detail: First reading June 18 (R19-128, unanimous). After the July 16 hearing, a motion to deny second reading failed 3-4 (R19-151) and second reading carried 4-3 (R19-152); third reading carried 4-3 on Aug 20 (R19-169) and the variance 5-2 (R19-170). Objections were below the new Municipal Board threshold.
figures: 8 units: 4 one-bedroom, 4 three-bedroom (minutes 6.5); site width 70 ft vs. 75 ft (minutes); developer-claimed value of a rezoning 'about $45,000' per door (objector M.J., transcript 0:27:04).
reasons: neighbourhood-not-ready: Community plan put the transitional multifamily zone on the north side of First Street; the south side was to stay single-family/duplex; approval sets a precedent for the next lots. (Jac Siemens); infrastructure-capacity: Drainage problems in the area; more hard surface from the variance. (Jac Siemens); neighbours-object: Applicant knew of neighbours' concerns but still required a variance. (Jake Hiebert)
public: Objectors J.B., T.B., M.J. (a local landlord-developer), L.W. (developer across the street) and J.G. (duplex neighbour) raised setbacks, privacy, traffic, the 75-ft minimum and the precedent for the south side; a letter from M.D. and W.D. also objected. The applicants (D.H. and S.H.) said they had canvassed all 16 owner-occupants.
mover: R19-152/R19-169 Michael Zwaagstra; R19-151 Jac Siemens; R19-170 Damian Penner
seconder: R19-152/R19-169 Damian Penner; R19-151 Jake Hiebert; R19-170 Susan Penner
vote: 4-3 (against: Siemens, J. Hiebert, B. Hiebert); variance 5-2 (against: Siemens, J. Hiebert)
notes: Bill Hiebert's reasons are not quoted: the 'Councillor Hebert' turns in these files could not be tied to Bill vs. Jake with certainty except where the minutes settle it (Jake seconded R19-151; only Jake and Siemens opposed the variance).

title: 8-unit apartment at 216 Hanover Street denied for lack of neighbourhood consultation
summary: A developer sought a conditional use to build an 8-unit, all-residential apartment (no main-floor commercial) on a C-1 neighbourhood-commercial lot at Hanover and Elm, citing a 1.3% rental vacancy rate. Neighbours objected to the scale, tree loss and fit with the single-family street. Council unanimously denied both the conditional use and the variance, saying the developer had not consulted the neighbourhood and that the vote was 'not a no to any future development there'.
status_detail: Conditional use CU-2019-03 denied (R19-140, Zwaagstra/Siemens) and variance V-2019-13 denied (R19-141, Zwaagstra/J. Hiebert), both unanimous. Council noted the applicant could not reapply for a year.
figures: 8 two-bedroom units; CMHC vacancy 1.3% cited by the applicant (transcript 0:08:31).
reasons: no-consultation: Applicant skipped the neighbourhood consultation earlier developers did; council would not redesign the project on the fly. (Michael Zwaagstra); neighbours-object: Strong, well-reasoned neighbourhood concerns; residential in C-1 is discretionary. (Michael Zwaagstra); neighbourhood-not-ready: Transition should go from the outside in, not leapfrog into a single-family area. (Jake Hiebert)
public: Neighbours (J.D. and others) objected to the scale, a large parking lot, tree loss and property values; the applicant (B.R., Winnipeg) cited the 1.3% vacancy rate and demand from retirees.
seconder: R19-140 Jac Siemens; R19-141 Jake Hiebert
notes: Jake Hiebert's stance comes from the minutes (seconder of R19-141) and a turn addressed 'Councillor Hebert'; the diarization label for that turn is shared with others, so it is not quoted. Speaker G ('Councillor Pinner', probably Susan Penner) said she had also voted against multifamily on Hanover behind the library; not quoted because the Penner could not be confirmed.

title: Residential and non-residential capital development fee by-laws adopted
summary: Council passed By-Law 2127 (residential capital development fees) and By-Law 2128 (non-residential) in November 2019, the city's main tool for having new development pay toward roads, sidewalks and other growth infrastructure. The meetings were not transcribed, so the debate and fee amounts are not on record here.
status_detail: First readings Nov 5 (R19-214, R19-215); second and third readings Nov 19, 2019 (R19-224 to R19-227); all unanimous.
figures: Fee amounts not in the minutes. 2018 year-end transfers show $675,000 of net development fee revenue to the capital development reserve and $35,225 of water and sewer impact fees (R19-074, 2019-03-19). In January 2021 the sidewalk capital development fee for a single-family lot was $1,610 (R21-012, outside this period).
seconder: D. Penner (R19-214); Zwaagstra (R19-215, R19-226); J. Hiebert (R19-224); B. Hiebert (R19-225); Siemens (R19-227)
notes: No transcripts exist for Nov 5 or Nov 19, 2019 and no agenda packages for 2019-2020, so the fee schedule could not be verified.

title: Clearspring Greens pathway: who pays for services in an old low-service subdivision
summary: Residents of Clearspring Greens, a rural-residential (low-service) subdivision, objected to paying most of a $625,000 connecting pathway as a local improvement, arguing development fees had not been collected from their developer. Michael Zwaagstra said the low-service zoning was created by earlier councils to make lots more affordable but should never have been allowed, and has been removed so future neighbourhoods get full urban services. Council moved the lighting cost to the capital development reserve.
status_detail: First and second readings carried 5-2 on Jan 7 (R20-004, R20-005) after a Siemens/J. Hiebert scope-reduction amendment failed 2-5 (R20-003); on Jan 21 lighting moved to the capital development reserve, 6-1 (R20-012). The plan was replaced in 2021 with a cheaper 50/50 version (R21-012, outside this period).
figures: $625,000 total, 146 lots (taxes-spending 2019-2020 file, transcript 2020-01-07); $208,000 lighting moved to the capital development reserve (R20-012).
reasons: fairness-precedent: Low-service zoning was a historic mistake; city residents should have full urban services, which cost money. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: Clearspring Greens residents said they paid market prices for low-service lots and that development fees for pathways were not taken from their developer (2020-01-07 hearing).
vote: R20-004/005 5-2 (against: Siemens, J. Hiebert); R20-012 6-1 (against: Siemens)
notes: Covered in more detail in data/taxes-spending/raw/2019-2020.json; recorded here only for the growth-cost and affordable-lot policy point.

title: Millbrook Market secondary plan: a 20-acre mixed-use district with 30-40% multifamily
summary: Council adopted a secondary plan (By-Law 2136) and rezoning (By-Law 2137) for Millbrook Market at 110 PTH 12 North, a 20-acre commercial mixed-use development where the owners expected 30-40% of the land to be multifamily, including possible 3-4 storey apartments and seniors' housing near amenities. In October council approved the subdivision and a variance letting residential buildings sit 10 ft from internal streets with parking behind.
status_detail: First readings Jan 7 (R20-007, R20-008); second/third readings March 3, 2020 (R20-042 to R20-045); subdivisions and front-yard variance V-2020-25 approved Oct 20, 2020 (R20-205, R20-206, R20-207). All unanimous.
figures: 20 acres; roughly 30-40% multifamily, 60-70% commercial; drawings showed 7 multifamily buildings (2020-03-03 transcript 0:18:55, owner K.U.); front setback 10 ft vs. 25 ft (2020-10-20 transcript 0:48:38).
reasons: market-decides: The best projects come from private developers, not government. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: Owners (D.B., K.U.) presented; no objections.

title: Parkhill Phase 2 re-planned for more duplexes, fourplexes and a high-density site
summary: At the developer's request (Sincerus Parkhill), council repealed the old Parkhill secondary plan and rezoned Phase 2 from mostly single-family to a mix of 28 single-family, 15 low-density, 16 medium-density lots and one high-density lot. The developer's representative said more attached homes on smaller lots would be an affordable alternative to renting. A neighbour objected that nearby Bush Farm Road would not be upgraded; staff said developers only build roads their lots front onto.
status_detail: First reading Feb 4 (R20-024); By-Law 2143 (repeal) second/third readings, By-Law 2140 second/third readings and subdivision 8250 all approved March 3, 2020 (R20-046 to R20-050), unanimous. Council members asked to study north-end road capacity at the July study session.
figures: 28 RSF, 15 RLD, 16 RMD lots and 1 RHD lot (2020-03-03 transcript 0:27:18, City Manager).
reasons: market-decides: Developers adjusting plans to market demand is what private development does well. (Bill Hiebert)
public: G.H. (Bush Farm Road resident and business owner) objected to all three files over road upgrades; the developer's representative (J.S.) said there is no subsidy but smaller attached homes let well-employed buyers own instead of rent.
notes: The Penner who asked for a July study session on north-end traffic (label L, 0:47:36) is not identified.

title: Maplewood Street rezoned for a 72-unit garden-apartment infill after earlier proposals failed
summary: By-Law 2147 rezoned 135-191 Maplewood Street from RLD to RMD for a 72-unit garden-style apartment complex built in phases of two 12-plexes. Earlier proposals on this stretch had been turned down after neighbourhood opposition; this developer consulted extensively, needed no variances and drew almost no objections. Councillors said deep old lots are too costly to redevelop one house at a time and noted vacancy stays low no matter how many units are approved.
status_detail: First reading April 7 (R20-077, Siemens/B. Hiebert); second reading after the May 19 hearing (Siemens/Zwaagstra, carried; no minutes on file for May 19); third reading July 7, 2020 subject to a development agreement (R20-137, Siemens/J. Hiebert). Building permits for two 12-unit buildings on Maplewood ($3.4M) were reported Dec 15, 2020.
figures: 72 units in 3 phases of two 12-plexes (2020-05-19 transcript, applicant J.P.); two 12-unit Maplewood buildings, $3.4M in permits (2020-12-15 transcript 0:42:29).
public: K.B. (Home Street North) raised drainage and loss of green space; few other objections. The applicant (J.P.) described the project as infill to revive an older neighbourhood.
resolution_no: R20-077; (May 19 second reading, no minutes); R20-137
seconder: R20-077 Bill Hiebert; May 19 Michael Zwaagstra; R20-137 Jake Hiebert
notes: A Councillor Hiebert (label L, addressed 'Councillor Ebert') raised traffic and school-bus concerns; not quoted because it could be either Hiebert. The minutes tie Jake Hiebert to R20-137.

title: 78 First Street rezoned for a second 10-unit building; '82 multifamily units' approved on the street
summary: By-Law 2148 rezoned 78 First Street (south side) to RMD so the builder of a 10-unit building next door could add a copy of it. Neighbours raised traffic and one argued the new units, at about $1,000 a month, are not affordable for vulnerable people. The City Manager said council had approved 82 multifamily units on First Street in a couple of years. Council approved unanimously; Michael Zwaagstra said rents are 'completely out of our purview', and Jac Siemens, while supporting it, said council had changed the community plan 'one lot at a time' and should revisit First Street.
status_detail: First reading May 5 (R20-097); second and third readings June 16, 2020 (R20-127 Zwaagstra/Siemens; R20-128 J. Hiebert/D. Penner), unanimous; 4-5 objections, below the Municipal Board threshold. A $1.5M 10-plex permit on First Street was reported Nov 17, 2020 (probably this building).
figures: 10 units; 82 multifamily units approved on First Street before this file (transcript 0:31:47, City Manager); rents about $1,000/month (resident C.S., 0:20:28).
reasons: market-decides: Rents are set by the market and outside council's purview; residents usually complain new apartments aren't high-end enough. (Michael Zwaagstra); market-decides: Side-by-sides or single-family homes don't pay the bills on costly older lots. (Earl Funk)
public: C.S. (First Street) objected that $1,000 rents are unaffordable for vulnerable people and suggested side-by-sides renting under $1,000; F. and I. (nearby residents) raised traffic and park safety; L.R. objected generally.
mover: R20-097/R20-127 Michael Zwaagstra; R20-128 Jake Hiebert
seconder: R20-097 Damian Penner; R20-127 Jac Siemens; R20-128 Damian Penner
notes: The Nov 17, 2020 permit report names 'a 10-plex multifamily building on First Street' without an address; linking it to 78 First Street is an inference.

title: 6-unit rental at 14 Ellis Avenue denied as 'too aggressive' for the lot
summary: Local applicants sought to rezone 14 Ellis Avenue to RMD for two triplexes (6 units), pitched as affordable rentals and citing a 1.2% vacancy rate. Several neighbours objected (drainage, traffic, parking, privacy, and the 'type of people' in lower-income rentals); the applicants stressed it was not low-income housing. Council unanimously denied second reading, saying six units on a narrow lot could not meet the infill policy, though several said RMD itself was acceptable there and invited a reworked plan.
status_detail: First reading July 7 (R20-136, Zwaagstra/Siemens); second reading denied Aug 18, 2020 (R20-156, Zwaagstra/J. Hiebert), unanimous; variance V-2020-17 not dealt with. No revised application found in 2020.
figures: 6 units in 2 two-storey triplexes; lot 71.5 ft vs. 75 ft required; CMHC 2019 vacancy 1.2% (Winkler 0.8%) cited by the applicant (transcript 0:07:31).
reasons: neighbourhood-not-ready: Six units on a narrow lot can't fit the street's character or pass the infill policy; also needed a variance. (Michael Zwaagstra); neighbourhood-not-ready: Not a transition from the edge; would put rentals behind neighbours' houses mid-block. (Jake Hiebert); infrastructure-capacity: Drainage problems in older low areas get pushed onto neighbours. (Jac Siemens); neighbours-object: Too aggressive in size; urged the developer to rework it. (Earl Funk)
public: Objectors B.T., G.P., E.W., L.G., P.S., M.G. and others cited drainage, traffic on a bus route, parking, setbacks, privacy and loss of green space; some linked 'lower-income rentals' to crime (unproven). Applicants (K.M. and partners) said it was 'not a low-income housing project' but aimed at people who can't afford $1,400 rents.
seconder: R20-136 Jac Siemens; R20-156 Jake Hiebert
notes: Damian Penner may be the 'Councilor Carra' speaker (label E, 1:04:37), but label E is also the City Manager in this file, so it is not quoted.

title: Developers' requests to lower high-density lots on Woodhaven and Lunn to medium density approved
summary: Three by-laws (2153, 2155, 2159) rezoned new lots on Woodhaven Avenue and Lunn Road from RHD (up to about 8 storeys) to RMD so developers could build lower, wider apartment buildings such as two 21-unit buildings. Councillors noted it was unusual to be asked to reduce density but agreed it made sense. Neighbours on Whitby Crescent asked for a privacy fence; the mayor said fences are not usually required in new (non-infill) development.
status_detail: By-Law 2153 first reading July 21 (R20-145), second/third Aug 18 (R20-157, R20-158); By-Law 2155 first reading Sept 1 (R20-166), second/third Oct 6 (R20-184, R20-185); By-Law 2159 first reading Oct 6 (R20-188), second/third Nov 3, 2020 (R20-217, R20-218). All unanimous, subject to development agreements.
figures: Two 21-unit apartment buildings planned at 216/220 Woodhaven (2020-08-18 transcript 1:12:25, applicant); RHD allows 8 storeys vs. RMD about 3-4 (2020-11-03 transcript 0:59:23, Mayor).
public: C.S. (Whitby Crescent) presented 12 neighbours' signatures asking for a privacy fence and saying residents were not 'overjoyed' about apartment blocks behind their homes; not a formal objection.

title: Dwelling Units Safety Standards By-law introduced to bring secondary suites and rentals up to basic safety
summary: Council gave first reading to By-Law 2157, setting minimum life-safety standards (smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, direct exit) for dwelling units, aimed especially at secondary suites built without permits. Jac Siemens said the city does not know where all secondary suites are and that upgrades could push some rents up; Susan Penner and the mayor said everyone has a right to safe housing and compliance would take a decade or two.
status_detail: First reading Sept 1, 2020 (R20-167, Siemens/S. Penner, unanimous); second and third readings Jan 5, 2021 (R21-007, R21-008, unanimous), just after this period.
figures: Vacancy 'below 4%' (transcript 0:21:02, Siemens); report to council dated May 12, 2020 (same).
reasons: cost: Upgrading substandard suites may raise rents for the tenants now living in them. (Jac Siemens)
notes: The by-law regulates safety; it does not legalize or encourage new secondary suites.

title: Four-storey, 24-unit condo with main-floor parking allowed at 530 Wilson Street
summary: Council approved a height variance (V-2020-28) letting a 24-unit condominium building on an already-RMD lot at 530 Wilson Street rise four storeys instead of three so parking could go inside on the main floor rather than in a surface lot. A neighbour objected in writing; Jac Siemens added a condition for large-caliper trees along the east boundary.
status_detail: Approved Nov 17, 2020 (moved by Zwaagstra, seconded by a Councillor Penner, with Siemens' friendly amendment for 2-inch caliper trees); no minutes on file for this meeting, so the resolution number is unknown.
figures: 24 units; 4 storeys vs. 3 permitted in RMD; site rezoned to RMD in 2014 (transcript 0:05:31, City Manager).
public: Neighbours at 534 Wilson objected in writing (height, privacy, traffic); the applicant's representative (Spanwest Housing Corporation for owner Steinbach Housing Inc.) described a 'luxury condo' still conscious of affordability.
notes: Jake Hiebert was absent (excused).

title: 24-unit First Street rezoning refused at first reading on staff advice, over both Penners' objections
summary: By-Law 2165 would have rezoned 85 First Street plus the back of 79 First Street for 24 more units. Staff recommended denying first reading (bad lot configuration, worse drainage, concept not meeting the infill policy) and noted council had already permitted up to 92 multifamily units on the street. Michael Zwaagstra and Jac Siemens carried the denial; Damian Penner and Susan Penner argued the questions should be aired at a public hearing.
status_detail: Motion to deny first reading carried Nov 17, 2020 (Zwaagstra/Siemens). No minutes are on file for this meeting; the transcript shows both Penners speaking against the motion but the count was not read out. Jake Hiebert was absent.
figures: 24 proposed units; up to 92 multifamily units already permitted on First Street (transcript 1:09:17, City Manager); 79 First Street is 45 ft wide (same).
reasons: infrastructure-capacity: City engineer said redevelopment would worsen drainage on 79 First Street. (Michael Zwaagstra); neighbourhood-not-ready: Creates a flag lot and a tiny single-family lot between multifamily; concept fails the infill policy; neighbour objections certain. (Michael Zwaagstra); study-first: Council needs a big-picture view of First Street; back-lane access was imposed by a Municipal Board ruling. (Jac Siemens)
vote: carried; Damian Penner and Susan Penner spoke against (count not recorded)
notes: Whether the two Penners voted against cannot be confirmed without minutes. Susan Penner is identified by elimination (label C, addressed 'Councillor Pinner', refers to 'Councillor Penner' = Damian), so her position is medium confidence and not quoted.

title: Parking and height relief granted to market apartment projects, twice against staff advice
summary: Council approved every apartment parking or height variance before it in 2021–2022. These were a narrower parkade aisle at Steinbach Housing Inc.'s 24-unit building on Wilson Street (staff had recommended denial), 213 instead of 236 stalls for a four-building complex at Millbrook Market, a fourth storey (basement suites) for 16 units at 71 Chrysler Gate, and 568 instead of 586 stalls at 6 Langill Way. Members argued tenants and developers know their own needs and that 1.5 stalls per unit overstates need for small units.
status_detail: V-2020-30 approved Jan 5, 2021 (R21-003 Zwaagstra/Siemens); V-2021-15 approved Jul 6, 2021 (R21-142 Zwaagstra/D. Penner); V-2021-25 approved Dec 7, 2021 (R21-252 Zwaagstra/B. Hiebert); V-2022-13 approved Aug 16, 2022 (R22-193 S. Penner/D. Penner). All unanimous. The zoning by-law's parking standard itself was not changed.
figures: V-2020-30: 18 ft aisle vs 22 ft required, 24 units. V-2021-15: 213 vs 236 stalls. V-2021-25: 4 storeys vs 3 allowed, 2 buildings × 8 units. V-2022-13: 568 vs 586 stalls; 14 micro and 120 one-bedroom units among them (D. Penner, 2022-08-16 0:10:53). Requirement: 1.5 stalls per unit + 10% visitors (S. Penner, 2022-03-01 0:55:17).
public: At 71 Chrysler Gate a neighbour (E.W.) raised privacy and school-traffic safety; the applicant offered fencing. No one objected to the other three.
seconder: Jac Siemens; Damian Penner (2); Bill Hiebert
notes: The Wilson Street building is owned by Steinbach Housing Inc.; whether it is market or non-profit housing was not stated. The Langill Way building's unit count is not stated in the minutes.

title: Clearspring Greens pathway: older subdivision charged the same $1,610 a new lot pays for sidewalks
summary: Clearspring Greens was built without a sidewalk connection, before the city collected a sidewalk capital development fee on new lots. After 78 objections stalled an earlier plan, Councillor Susan Penner moved to drop the lighting and split the path cost 50/50, capping each parcel at $1,610, the same sidewalk fee a new lot pays in 2021, with the city's half from the capital development reserve. Objections fell to six and the local improvement by-law passed.
status_detail: R21-011 cancelled the old plan and R21-012 adopted the revised one (S. Penner/Siemens, unanimous, Jan 5, 2021). By-law 2168 got first and second reading Feb 16, 2021 (R21-032 S. Penner/Siemens; R21-033 Siemens/J. Hiebert) and third reading Apr 20, 2021 (R21-076 Siemens/J. Hiebert), all unanimous.
