figures: Residential capital development fee for sidewalks $1,610 per single-family lot in 2021 under By-law 2127 (Warkentin, 2021-01-05 0:34:58). Earlier plan ~$4,200 per parcel, then ~$2,850 (0:34:03). Project ~$623,000 with lights, $463,000 without; 145-146 parcels (S. Penner 0:35:38). Minutes Feb 16, 2021: $650,000 project, 50% levied on 145 benefiting properties up to $1,610 ($392.66/yr for 5 years).
reasons: fairness-precedent: $1,610 is fair because it equals what any buyer of a new lot pays for sidewalks (Susan Penner)
public: 78 objections were filed against the first plan (2020). At the Feb 16, 2021 hearing, 7 letters objected and 1 supported; a resident (T.B.) who had objected withdrew his objection at the podium.
notes: Included because it shows who pays when growth-related infrastructure is not funded at development; it is a pathway project rather than housing. The Feb 16 Councillor Hiebert remarks are not attributed (two Hieberts, labels unclear).

title: Dwelling Safety Standards By-law 2157 passed to set minimum safety rules for secondary suites
summary: Council gave second and third reading to By-law 2157, which sets minimum life-safety standards (smoke and carbon monoxide alarms, a safe exit) for dwelling units, aimed mainly at secondary suites. Staff said compliance would mostly be voluntary, with inspections on request from owners or tenants. Councillors framed it as protecting tenants; no one raised the risk of losing low-cost suites.
status_detail: Second reading R21-007 (Zwaagstra/Siemens) and third reading R21-008 (Siemens/J. Hiebert), both unanimous, Jan 5, 2021. First reading had been given Sept 1, 2020 (per staff).
figures: Upgrades estimated at plus or minus $3,000 per suite if all were needed; about 500 hours of city staff time in the first year (Siemens, transcript 0:25:16); about a dozen public comments, mostly in favour (Warkentin, 0:26:48).
public: Staff reported an online engagement in 2020 (video, several hundred views) with about a dozen comments, mostly supportive. No delegations.
notes: By-law text not reviewed; description from the council discussion. Effects on the supply of low-cost suites were not discussed in 2021 (the issue resurfaced in 2024 per the existing report).

title: Record growth and housing affordability noted, with no city housing strategy proposed
summary: Monthly building-permit reports showed multi-family units outpacing single-family homes. Members celebrated developer confidence and, by mid-2022, over 1,000 new units since 2018. Damian Penner said home ownership was slipping out of reach for young families, but blamed federal policy and proposed nothing local. In 2021–2022 no councillor proposed a city housing strategy, needs assessment, affordability target or incentive. The only affordable-housing action was passing on the provincial grant.
status_detail: Permit reports were received as information each month. No local housing-affordability policy was proposed or referred in this period (searched for 'housing strategy', 'needs assessment', 'accelerator', 'CMHC').
figures: 2020: 200 multi-family and 100 single/two-family units, '302 new families' (councillor, 2021-01-19 0:09:28). Jan–Oct 2021: 93 single/two-family and 100 multi-family units (2021-11-16 0:15:57). November 2021: 20 single-family + 54 multi-family = 74 units (Mayor, 2021-12-07 0:53:02). 'Over 1,000 new housing units' since 2018 (B. Hiebert, 2022-07-05 0:00:14).
reasons: other-governments-fund: housing affordability tied to federal fiscal policy and inflation (Damian Penner); market-decides: growth seen as developer- and market-led (several members)
notes: The 2021-01-19 and 2021-11-16 permit remarks are not quoted: the Jan 19 speaker is not identified, and on Nov 16 both Councillors Penner spoke on the motion.

title: 107 First Street rezoned for an 18-unit infill apartment project
summary: Kingdom Home Building Inc. asked to rezone 107 First Street from RLD to RMD for 18 two-storey rental units on a large older lot. Staff noted several First Street lots had been redeveloped into multi-family since 2018 and recommended approval. One neighbour objected in writing; no one spoke against it. Council approved unanimously, with Councillor Zwaagstra arguing medium density is the only economically feasible way to redevelop such lots.
status_detail: First reading May 18, 2021 (R21-109 Siemens/S. Penner); second and third reading Jun 15, 2021 (R21-128 Zwaagstra/S. Penner; R21-129 S. Penner/J. Hiebert), subject to a development agreement. All unanimous.
figures: 18 units (staff, 2021-06-15 0:04:59). Applicant said it had built nearly 110 multi-family units since 2018 with almost 0% vacancy (0:06:59).
public: One letter of objection from neighbours on First Street (G.B. and C.B.); Manitoba's Community Planning Branch raised no concerns. No one spoke against it at the hearing.

title: Langill Farm (Park Road West): 68-acre mixed neighbourhood with single-family to high-density lots approved
summary: Penn-Co Construction (through HTFC Planning and Design) proposed a 68-acre neighbourhood west of Clearspring Mall. It has single-family, low-, medium- and high-density lots, parks and a commercial strip, including Penn-Co's new head office. Council amended the OCP, rezoned the land and approved the subdivision unanimously with no objections. Revisions followed: six multi-family lots were merged into one parcel, and more land was moved from medium to high density.
status_detail: OCP By-law 2183 second reading Aug 17, 2021 and third reading Nov 2, 2021 after ministerial approval. Rezoning By-law 2184 second reading Aug 17 (R21-175) and third reading Oct 19, 2021 (R21-224). Subdivision 4451-2021-8466 approved Aug 17 (R21-174 D. Penner/B. Hiebert) and revised Dec 21, 2021 (R21-271). By-law 2191 (RMD→RHD, RHD→C3) second and third reading Jan 18, 2022 (R22-015, R22-016). All unanimous, subject to development agreements. Sod turning reported May 17, 2022.
figures: Subdivision: 46 RSF, 82 RLD, 5 RMD and 6 RHD lots plus a bareland condominium, 139 residential parcels and 2 public reserves on ~68 acres (minutes Aug 17, 2021; Thiessen 0:20:06). Mayor said about 700 'doors' were planned (2022-05-17 0:00:54).
public: No objections. A neighbouring landowner's architect asked about a future road connection.

title: Assisted living for 20 residents approved on Beaver Crescent (former church lots)
summary: Three Way Builders Ltd. applied for a conditional use to build an assisted living facility on four lots at 11–17 Beaver Crescent bought by Silver Lining Care: two buildings of 10 units each for people needing home care. Two neighbours wrote with concerns; no one spoke at the hearing. Council approved unanimously, subject to a development agreement.
status_detail: Conditional Use CU-2021-03 approved Jul 6, 2021 (R21-141 S. Penner/Siemens, unanimous), subject to a development agreement. Construction not verified.
figures: 2 buildings × 10 units (minutes Jul 6, 2021).
public: Two letters voicing concerns from nearby residents (M.L. and C.L.; D.K.). No one attended to object.
notes: No transcript: the Jul 6, 2021 video failed to download, so this rests on the minutes only.

title: Hampton Village final phase (33 lots) approved over neighbours' traffic objections; upheld by the Municipal Board
summary: Stonebridge Development Corporation sought to rezone and subdivide the last phase of Hampton Village (33 single-family lots) off Wyndham Estate Drive. Residents objected over construction traffic, a single access and children's safety. One asked council to hold off until infrastructure was in place. Council approved unanimously, saying the phase followed the 2009 concept plan and lots were scarce, and promised more sidewalks. Enough objections forced a Municipal Board hearing, after which council gave third reading.
status_detail: First reading Jul 20, 2021 (R21-156). Second reading Aug 17, 2021 (R21-176 Zwaagstra/D. Penner) and subdivision approval (R21-177 J. Hiebert/B. Hiebert), unanimous. Municipal Board hearing Mar 16–17, 2022 (R22-057). Third reading May 17, 2022 (R22-129 Zwaagstra/D. Penner, unanimous); the board imposed no conditions. Sidewalks on Ashford/Wyndham were in the 2022 capital plan; the rest of Wyndham was not yet budgeted (staff, 0:53:35).
figures: 33 RSF lots and a public reserve (minutes). The 120-lots-per-access policy would be exceeded, with 128 properties on one access (staff, 2021-08-17 0:42:04, 1:02:35). Eight letters plus a 58-name submission (minutes).
reasons: market-decides: new lots are needed so people (and their children) can afford to live in Steinbach; low inventory (Michael Zwaagstra); already-doing-enough: sidewalks will be added over time; growth pains are temporary (Mayor Earl Funk)
public: Residents of Wyndham Estate Drive and Preston Place (including A.B., E.B., C.H. and R.C.) objected over construction traffic, speed, one access point, school bus stops and missing sidewalks. One asked council to hold the 33 lots until infrastructure was in place. The developer's representative (C.P.) said the city is 'bursting at the seams' and that construction parking would move off Wyndham.
notes: Resident initials are taken from the transcript's spelling of self-introduced names and the minutes' list; 'R.C.' (78 Wyndham Estate Dr.) may be mis-transcribed.

title: 115 First Street added to the infill project (12 more units) despite traffic objections; 6–1 vote
summary: Kingdom Home Building Inc. asked to rezone 115 First Street (an uninhabitable house) to RMD and join it to 107 First Street, adding two buildings and 12 units for about 30 in total. Two residents objected over traffic, parking, trees and green space. Councillors Siemens and Jake Hiebert raised the need for a traffic impact study. Jake Hiebert moved to deny it (no seconder), and council approved 6–1.
status_detail: First reading Aug 3, 2021 (R21-169 Siemens/D. Penner, unanimous). Sept 7, 2021: J. Hiebert's motion to deny got no seconder; second reading R21-187 (Zwaagstra/Siemens) and third reading R21-188 (Siemens/B. Hiebert) carried 6–1, J. Hiebert against. No separate traffic impact study was ordered; members pointed to the city's annual October traffic counts.
figures: 12 added units, about 30 in total on the two lots (staff/applicant, 2021-09-07 0:18:05–0:19:04). A resident said 92 apartment homes were built on that block of First Street in the past 3 years (0:20:03). Only 2 registered objections, too few for a Municipal Board referral (Warkentin, 0:41:17).
reasons: study-first: wanted further multi-family on First Street to stop until a traffic study was done (Jake Hiebert); infrastructure-capacity: First Street is filling with RMD and traffic needs study; did not insist, to avoid delaying construction (Jac Siemens)
public: W.N. (a developer and owner of a nearby building) objected over traffic and parking, saying the block had seen 92 apartment homes in 3 years and 'the limit is the limit'. S.C. objected over traffic, trees and the loss of green space. The applicant said its buildings have zero vacancy.
notes: Siemens's Sept 7 remarks (0:35:46–0:37:15) are split across labels E and F (F is also the city manager), so they are paraphrased, not quoted.

title: Routine growth approvals: estate lots, duplex and multi-family lots, and 62 entry-level lots
summary: Council unanimously approved a series of uncontested greenfield files. These were 37 estate lots on Harmony Lane (By-law 2189), six of those lots rezoned for two-family homes (By-law 2193), five Lexington Village lots rezoned to medium density for multi-family (By-law 2176), the final 62-lot entry-level phase on Essex Drive and Sesame Street, and a bareland condominium subdivision. Members described the demand as market-driven and praised entry-level price points.
status_detail: By-law 2189 and Subdivision 4451-2021-8494 approved Oct 19, 2021 (R21-217/218/219). By-law 2176 second reading Jan 18, 2022 (R22-017), third reading Feb 15, 2022 (R22-048). By-law 2193 second and third reading Feb 15, 2022 (R22-034/035). Subdivision 4451-2021-8555 (62 lots) Feb 15, 2022 (R22-033 S. Penner/Zwaagstra). Subdivision 4451-2021-8509 (bareland condo) Feb 15, 2022 (R22-047). Condominium plan at 49 Clear Springs Rd E Jul 6, 2021 (R21-145). All unanimous.
figures: Harmony Lane phase 11: 37 RSF lots; Lexington Village: 5 RMD lots, ~200 existing units of mixed types (developer, 2022-01-18 0:17:53); Essex/Sesame: 62 residential lots (minutes Feb 15, 2022).
reasons: market-decides: developers seek rezonings as they learn what sells (several members)
public: Drainage concerns from a Hespeler Street South neighbour (K.B./G.B.) on Harmony Lane; no other objections.
notes: Grouped routine files; none had a divided vote.

title: 14 Ellice Avenue fourplex approved after a 2020 denial and a neighbourhood petition
summary: After council denied a six-unit building at 14 Ellice Avenue in August 2020, the owners returned with a fourplex designed to look like a duplex, with deeper yards, two stalls per unit and no side windows. Neighbours filed letters and a 21-signature petition, worrying it would set a precedent for bigger buildings. Council approved it unanimously, praising the developer for listening to the neighbourhood, and granted a lot-width variance.
status_detail: First reading Sept 21, 2021 (R21-206 D. Penner/B. Hiebert). Second reading Oct 19, 2021 (R21-221 Siemens/Zwaagstra). Third reading Dec 21, 2021 (R21-272 Siemens/Zwaagstra) once staff found too few objections for a Municipal Board referral; Variance V-2021-20 (71.5 ft lot width vs 75 ft) approved (R21-273 Siemens/B. Hiebert). All unanimous.
figures: 4 units (two 3-bedroom, two 1-bedroom), 2 stalls per unit, rear yard 62 ft vs 25 ft required (applicant, 2021-10-19 0:24:12). Petition of 21 signatures from 18 properties (minutes).
public: E.W. and K.W. (next door) and others on Ellice Avenue and Autumnwood Drive objected in writing and with a petition. E.W. feared the project 'sets the bar' for denser development, citing First Street. B.C. (next door) objected over quiet and the garbage location. The applicant (R.P.) said the rents would not be 'affordable or lower rent'.
notes: Minutes list the applicant as Rick Penner, a private developer (no relation to council members is stated).

title: Provincial $1.34M affordable-housing grant passed to Steinbach Community Outreach for 24 units (The Bridge)
summary: In March 2021 the province gave the city a conditional $1.337M grant for affordable housing. Three proposals came in: an 18-unit building on First Street, a Habitat for Humanity duplex, and a 24-unit Steinbach Community Outreach (SCO) building. Staff recommended forwarding both Habitat's and SCO's, but council sent only SCO's to MHRC so it would get the full amount. In 2022 council awarded the grant and passed By-law 2210, structuring it as a forgivable 20-year second mortgage to keep the units affordable. The city added no money of its own.
status_detail: Recommendation to MHRC Nov 2, 2021 (R21-232 Zwaagstra/S. Penner, unanimous); MHRC approval letter Dec 9, 2021. Grant of $1,337,500 awarded Jul 5, 2022 (R22-161 Siemens/Zwaagstra, unanimous). By-law 2210 first and second reading Jul 5, 2022 (R22-163 Siemens/S. Penner; R22-164 D. Penner/Siemens) and third reading Aug 2, 2022. The project moved from 330 Stonebridge Crossing to 224 Woodhaven Avenue after Bridgepark Manor kept its land for seniors' housing; per the existing report The Bridge opened in late 2023. Habitat's duplex was not funded.
figures: Grant $1,337,500 (Thiessen, 2022-07-05 0:05:15). 24 units: 12 bachelor (400 sq ft) and 12 one-bedroom (600 sq ft); rent $583 / $801 including utilities; income caps $23,500 / $32,000; 20-year affordability; project cost estimated $3.6M in Nov 2021 (Siemens, 0:06:23). SCO had raised $350,000 and pledged over $700,000 (Mayor, 2021-11-02 0:14:42).
reasons: other-governments-fund: the grant comes from the province; the city's role is to pick the best proposal (Michael Zwaagstra); cost: splitting the grant would leave neither project fully funded (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: SCO (executive director I.K.) said its clients often live in basement suites and cannot afford cars; SCO helps 765 people a year. Habitat for Humanity Southeast Chapter's duplex proposal had no site chosen.
notes: The 18-unit First Street proposal (Proposal 1) was from a private builder; its name is spelled 'Vought Building' in the transcript and was not verified.

title: Two-acre split of unserviced reserve land on Hespeler Street South denied to protect future servicing
summary: Owners of a 6.75-acre unserviced lot at 524 Hespeler Street South (zoned DR-1, development reserve) asked to split off a 2-acre house lot. Staff recommended denial under the policy of keeping reserve land in large holdings until services arrive. Council agreed unanimously: large rural lots would make it costly to extend water and sewer later and would 'leapfrog' orderly development.
status_detail: Denied Nov 16, 2021 (R21-238 Siemens/D. Penner, unanimous).
figures: 6.75-acre parcel split into 2 acres + 4.75 acres; DR-1 minimum 20 acres; no city water or sewer (Warkentin, 0:19:03; Siemens 0:20:32).
reasons: infrastructure-capacity: no city services; would leapfrog development and complicate future servicing (Jac Siemens); cost: very expensive to run services past a 2-acre frontage (Damian Penner)
public: The owners (applicant R.W. for H.K. and E.K.) did not speak; Siemens acknowledged landowners' frustration at having to wait for development.
notes: Status 'declined' records that council refused the application (a growth-management decision, not a refusal of housing policy).

title: Parking for The Bridge cut from 40 to 30 stalls, against staff advice, because low-income tenants own few cars
summary: SCO asked to build its 24-unit affordable building at 224 Woodhaven Avenue with 30 parking stalls instead of the 40 the zoning by-law requires. Staff recommended denying the reduction because Woodhaven has no street parking. SCO showed that comparable subsidized buildings use far fewer stalls. Council approved it unanimously, on condition that the site have only bachelor and one-bedroom suites and a grant agreement be signed. Members said this did not lower the rule for ordinary apartments.
status_detail: V-2022-02 approved Mar 1, 2022 (R22-052 Siemens/S. Penner, unanimous) with conditions: bachelor and one-bedroom suites only, a city grant agreement for affordable housing before a permit, and (friendly amendment) a development agreement. The general parking rule (1.5 stalls + 10% visitors per unit, regardless of unit size) was not changed.
figures: 30 stalls vs 40 required for 24 units (Warkentin, 0:13:37). Comparable buildings: Wilson Court uses 7 stalls for 24 units, Penfeld 15 for 24 (R.P., 0:34:10). 4 of 14 prospective tenants had a car (minutes).
reasons: parking-rules: acceptable precedent only for SCO-managed affordable housing, not for regular apartments (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: SCO's I.K. and R.P. explained that clients cannot afford cars and asked council to write lower parking for low-income housing into the by-law. A Whitby Crescent neighbour (N.P.) raised privacy, fencing, dumpsters and speeding along Woodhaven but did not object.
notes: R.P. is labelled G with low confidence in the speaker map because G merges with a councillor elsewhere; the quoted turn is inside his self-introduced presentation.

title: Old Tom Road / Loewen Boulevard neighbourhood (95 parcels, mixed density) approved over high-density and traffic objections
themes: subdivision; rezoning; density; apartments; development-agreement; growth-costs
summary: A developer (via Loewen Henderson Banman Legault LLP) proposed the first phase of a ~128-acre neighbourhood at Old Tom Road and Loewen Boulevard: 30 single-family, 60 low-density and 4 high-density lots plus commercial mixed use. Neighbours objected to the share of high density in phase 1, traffic on Old Tom Road, drainage and the lack of green space. Council approved it unanimously. Members said high density is needed for people who cannot afford houses, and that the developer pays for new neighbourhoods.
status_detail: First readings Jul 5, 2022. Sept 6, 2022: OCP By-law 2211, rezonings 2212 and 2213 given second reading and Subdivision 4451-2022-8586 approved (R22-201 to R22-205), unanimous. A notice error forced council to rescind 2213's second reading (R22-227, Oct 4) and rehear it; second reading again Nov 1, 2022 (R22-250 D. Penner/S. Penner), unanimous, after the RM of La Broquerie withdrew its objection. Third readings of 2211, 2212 and 2213 came Jun 6, 2023 (R23-115 to R23-117), outside this period.
figures: 95 parcels: 30 RSF, 60 RLD, 4 RHD, 1 C-MX, 2 public reserves (minutes Sept 6, 2022). Developer's representative said a $1.2–1.4M lift station would be paid by the developer (2022-09-06 1:05:38; label merged in map, so not quoted). Damian Penner at first reading: 'potentially 94 lots' (2022-07-05 0:19:16).
reasons: market-decides: move out of the way and let the market decide the mix (Damian Penner); market-decides: phasing follows supply and demand; developers won't build high density nobody rents (Susan Penner)
public: R.F. and D.E. (Loewen Boulevard) and J.C. objected, saying the area already has enough high density, Old Tom Road is used as a bypass, phase 1 is mostly high density with no green space, and the city should study traffic first and stick to its OCP. The RM of La Broquerie objected on drainage, then withdrew. D.E. urged council to plan for Loewen Boulevard traffic coming from Deerfield.
mover: Michael Zwaagstra / Jac Siemens / Susan Penner / Damian Penner
notes: In reply to J.C.'s remark that he hoped to be a developer one day, Councillor Susan Penner said 'Maybe when you're a developer, you'll change your mind.' (1:13:50). The Bill Hiebert remark at 1:20:40 (speaker label low confidence) is not used.

title: Fourplex at 205 McKenzie Avenue advanced 5–2 over 22 neighbours' objections; mayor and Siemens opposed
summary: Kingdom Home Building Inc. applied for the widowed owner of an older house across from the regional secondary school to rezone it to RMD for a four-unit building: her home, a three-bedroom townhome and two one-bedroom basement suites to rent. Twenty-two nearby owners objected over property values, precedent, privacy and school traffic. Siemens moved denial (no seconder). The majority said redeveloping big old lots only pays with more units and four units add little traffic. Siemens and Mayor Funk voted against, preferring a duplex.
status_detail: First reading Oct 4, 2022 (R22-231 Zwaagstra/B. Hiebert, unanimous). Nov 1, 2022: Siemens's motion to deny got no seconder; second reading R22-253 (Zwaagstra/D. Penner) carried 5–2 (Siemens, Funk against). The objections triggered a Municipal Board hearing (April 2023, R23-063) and third reading passed Jun 18, 2024, 6–1 (Siemens against), outside this period.
figures: 4 units, 7 stalls plus 2 garages; garage 45 ft from the sidewalk; lot 74 ft wide vs 75 ft (applicant, 2022-11-01 1:00:40, 1:17:51). 21 letters on file, 22 objectors per the residents' spokesman (0:58:15, 1:03:45).
reasons: neighbourhood-not-ready: 'not ready' for that kind of development in the area; a side-by-side might work (Mayor Earl Funk); neighbours-object: sides with the residents who know the busy area; a duplex makes more sense (Jac Siemens)
public: C.K. (Cottonwood Bend), speaking for most nearby owners, objected over property values, precedent in an RLD area, privacy, noise and school-area traffic. He asked council to delay 60–90 days and order a traffic study. A McKenzie Avenue resident (V.H.) raised children's safety and privacy. The applicant (L.W.) called it infill that helps an owner afford a new home and adds rentals.
notes: Existing 2022–2026 report records the later Municipal Board hearing and 6–1 final vote.

title: 6 First Street (22–24 units, 3 storeys beside PTH 52) advanced 5–2 over setback and character objections
summary: An applicant consolidating 6 First Street with a triangular strip of 78 PTH 52 West asked to redesignate the strip from industrial to central business district (OCP By-law 2216) and rezone both from RLD to RMD (By-law 2215) for a 3-storey, 22–24-unit building. Councillor Siemens moved to deny first reading (no seconder) and later voted against, joined by Jake Hiebert at second reading. Siemens wanted a 30-ft buffer from the highway and said it did not fit his vision for the area. The majority called it logical redevelopment that puts homes near jobs.
status_detail: Oct 4, 2022: Siemens's motion to deny first reading of By-law 2216 had no seconder; first reading R22-229 carried 6–1 (Siemens against); By-law 2215 first reading R22-230 unanimous. Nov 1, 2022: By-law 2216 second reading R22-251 and By-law 2215 second reading R22-252 carried 5–2 (Siemens, J. Hiebert against). Third readings came Jul 4, 2023 (2216 5–1, Siemens against; 2215 unanimous).
figures: 22–24 units, 3 storeys; corner-lot side yard moved from 5 to 8 ft from PTH 52 (staff/applicant, 2022-11-01 0:40:58, 0:33:00). About 100 multi-family units approved along First Street over the past 5 years (Warkentin, 0:40:58).
reasons: neighbourhood-not-ready: building would look out of place; wants a 30-ft highway buffer; CBD designation reduces council's say over setbacks (Jac Siemens)
public: Loewen Windows (J.S.) raised sight lines and setbacks near the highway approach. A neighbour (C.M.) asked about construction noise. A nearby owner and developer (L.W., Kingdom Home Building) did not oppose the rezoning but wanted buffers and frontage settled first. Swift Communications (E.S.) spoke in favour.
vote: 5-2 (against: Jac Siemens, Jake Hiebert); first reading of 2216 6-1 (against: Siemens)
notes: Jake Hiebert gave no stated reason for his votes against.

title: Sewer upgrades to open the east side for housing: Lift Station 2, Loewen force main, Lift Station 1 twinning
summary: Council borrowed $2M (By-law 2221) to upgrade Lift Station 2 on Loewen Boulevard and add a force main, saying east-side subdivisions could not develop until sewer capacity was added. It then awarded the construction tender (topping it up from the utility reserve fed by development fees), a 2024 Loewen Boulevard force main, and design of the Lift Station 1-to-lagoon force main twinning, for which it asked the Manitoba Water Services Board to share design costs.
status_detail: By-law 2221 given third reading Mar 21, 2023 (R23-054) after Municipal Board approval; tender awarded Oct 17, 2023 (R23-213); debenture By-law 2239 passed Mar 5, 2024 (R24-055); force main tender Mar 19, 2024 (R24-065); Water Services Board request Jun 18, 2024 (R24-127); twinning design awarded Nov 2024 (R24-209, amended R24-223).
figures: Lift Station 2: estimated $2.265M, $2M borrowed over 5 years at max 8%, remainder from utility reserve (transcript Jan 3, 2023, 0:11:29); low bid $1,996,642.57 plus about $250,000 from the utility reserve (minutes R23-213; transcript Oct 17, 2023, 0:22:35). Loewen Blvd force main $491,693 (R24-065). Lift station/force main twinning engineering $529,789.89 (R24-209, Nov 5, 2024), revised to $463,201 (R24-223, Nov 19, 2024).
public: No one spoke at the Jan 3, 2023 local-improvement hearing.
mover: Jac Siemens (first reading); Michael Zwaagstra (third reading, tender)
notes: The Lift Station 1 twinning resolutions of Nov 5, 2024 have no recording (minutes only).

title: 205 McKenzie Avenue fourplex across from the high school: Municipal Board hearing, then final approval 6-1
summary: After objections, rezoning By-law 2217 (a single-family lot across from the Steinbach Regional Secondary School, to allow a fourplex) went to the Manitoba Municipal Board. Council sent the City Manager and City Planner to represent the city at the April 2023 hearing. With the development agreement signed, council gave third reading in June 2024; Councillor Siemens voted against, citing school-zone congestion and parking.
status_detail: Municipal Board delegation approved Mar 21, 2023 (R23-063); third reading Jun 18, 2024, 6-1 (R24-129). First and second readings were in 2022.
figures: On-site parking for 7 vehicles (Siemens, 1:41:20).
reasons: infrastructure-capacity: Busy school crosswalk and full street parking; cars backing onto a busy street. (Jac Siemens)
public: Objections in 2022 triggered the Municipal Board referral (details outside this period).
notes: The Municipal Board's ruling is not in the council record; third reading after it implies the by-law was allowed to proceed.

title: Routine lot additions in built subdivisions (Millbrook Market, Gooseberry Drive, Hampton Village)
summary: Council approved several small subdivisions adding housing lots: four commercial mixed-use lots at Millbrook Market (expected to carry medium-density residential), three single/two-family lots from one lot on Gooseberry Drive (Agassiz Shore Developments), and an extra lot in Hampton Village by closing part of a city public reserve and selling the land to the developer (By-law 2237; subdivision subject to a purchase/sale agreement).
public: Hampton Village neighbours wrote two letters and one (D.M.) asked how closing the reserve benefits the city rather than the developer.
mover: Michael Zwaagstra; Michael Zwaagstra; Jac Siemens; Susan Penner; Susan Penner
seconder: Damian Penner; Bill Hiebert; Bill Hiebert; Jac Siemens; Michael Zwaagstra

title: Small-lot infill subdivision at 68 Brandt Street denied
summary: Owners (residents, identified by initials G.L. and R.L.) asked to split a large single-family lot on Brandt Street to create one new 31.5-foot-wide lot. Staff recommended denial, citing the OCP infill policy that infill be compatible with the neighbourhood in setback, height and character, and the provincial highway access concern. Council denied it unanimously.
status_detail: Subdivision 4451-2023-8813 denied Jun 6, 2023 (R23-114).
figures: Proposed lot 31.5 ft frontage x 160 ft (about 1/10 acre); neighbouring lots 82-125 ft wide (transcript 0:19:08, 0:23:24).
reasons: neighbourhood-not-ready: A 31.5-ft lot does not fit a street of 82-125 ft lots and fails the infill policy's compatibility test. (Jac Siemens; Jake Hiebert); infrastructure-capacity: Another driveway backing onto a busy four-lane provincial road (Brandt St / PTH 12). (Jac Siemens; Jake Hiebert)
public: No objectors spoke; the applicants are private owners (initials only).

title: East-side development at Loewen Blvd and Old Tom Road: OCP change and rezonings to commercial mixed-use and single-family to high-density residential
summary: Council gave third reading to an OCP amendment (By-law 2211) and two rezonings (By-laws 2212 and 2213) for a multi-phase development at Loewen Boulevard and Old Tom Road, after ministerial approval. Part of the land became commercial mixed-use (CMX) and the rest a mix of single-family (RSF), low-density (RLD) and high-density (RHD) residential, subject to a development agreement. Members said the city's earlier trunk sewer extension was built in anticipation of this growth.
status_detail: Third readings carried unanimously Jun 6, 2023 (R23-115, R23-116, R23-117); public hearings were held in Sept and Nov 2022 (outside this period).
public: No public comment at third reading (hearings were in 2022).
mover: Michael Zwaagstra; Damian Penner; Jac Siemens
seconder: Bill Hiebert; Michael Zwaagstra; Bill Hiebert
notes: Developer name not stated in the third-reading minutes.

title: Height and setback variances granted for apartment buildings (188 Lund Road, 48 Market Boulevard)
summary: Council let a multi-family building at 188 Lund Road count as four storeys (because its half-buried basement holds units) and allowed a 19-foot rear setback instead of 25 feet for a multi-family building at 48 Market Boulevard in the commercial mixed-use zone. The Lund Road developer said the zoning by-law's definition of a storey did not match the National Building Code.
status_detail: V-2023-07 approved Jun 20, 2023 (R23-124); V-2023-24 approved Dec 5, 2023 (R23-242); both unanimous.
figures: Lund Road building about 41.5 ft above grade vs 36.5 ft for a nearby 3-storey building (transcript 0:23:49).
public: A neighbouring owner (J.I.) asked about parking and said they felt 'closed in' but did not formally object.
notes: The Lund Road variance mover is B. Hiebert per minutes; the speaker map attributes the motion turn to Jake Hiebert, so no quote is taken from it.

title: 6 First Street: OCP change, rezoning and lane closing for a 22-24 unit apartment building
summary: Council completed approvals for a multi-family building of 22-24 units at 6 First Street beside PTH 52: an OCP amendment moving the site into the central business district (By-law 2216), rezoning from RLD to RMD (By-law 2215), a lot consolidation, and closing an unused public lane that is really a drain (By-law 2232). Councillor Siemens voted against the OCP change and the lane closing because CBD zoning allows building close to the highway with no setback; Councillor Jake Hiebert, who had objected to the building type earlier, also voted against the lane closing.
status_detail: OCP By-law 2216 third reading 5-1 (R23-141); rezoning By-law 2215 third reading unanimous (R23-142); subdivision approved (R23-143), all Jul 4, 2023; lane-closing By-law 2232 second and third readings 5-2 on Nov 7, 2023 (R23-226, R23-227).
figures: 22 to 24 units (City Manager, Jul 4, 2023, 0:19:02).
reasons: parking-rules: Objected that CBD zoning allows a zero lot line, letting a building sit too close to PTH 52 without council approval (a setback concern, not opposition to apartments). (Jac Siemens)
public: One written objection to the lane closing from a neighbouring landowner/developer (initials not given in the minutes extract) about rear access; staff said the strip has always been a drain and the lots have street access.
mover: Damian Penner (2216); Bill Hiebert (2215); Michael Zwaagstra (subdivision, 2232 second reading); Bill Hiebert (2232 third reading)
seconder: Jake Hiebert; Michael Zwaagstra; Damian Penner; Susan Penner; Michael Zwaagstra
vote: 2216: 5-1 (against: Siemens; S. Penner absent); 2215: unanimous; 2232: 5-2 (against: Siemens, J. Hiebert)
notes: Earlier readings and the public hearing for 6 First Street were in 2022 (outside this period).

title: 84 McKenzie Avenue: 70-lot mixed subdivision (single-family, duplex, townhouse, multi-family) approved
summary: Neustaedter Holdings rezoned about 17-20 acres on McKenzie Avenue from development reserve to RSF, RLD and RMD and subdivided it into 70 lots: smaller single-family lots, duplexes, townhouses and some multi-family sites, extending Lincoln Avenue and opening Sterling Crescent. The developer said engineers confirmed reserve servicing capacity. Council approved it unanimously, with Councillor Susan Penner describing it as meeting the needs of people who need affordable housing.
status_detail: By-law 2230 first reading Jul 4 (R23-138), second and third readings Aug 1, 2023 (R23-157, R23-158); subdivision approved Aug 1, 2023 (R23-159).
figures: 70 lots: 14 RMD, 12 RLD, 44 single-family, 3 public reserves (Siemens, transcript 0:22:13; minutes).
public: A neighbour backing onto the site (N.T.) asked about setbacks and lot sizes and regretted losing open space; no formal objections.
mover: Jake Hiebert; Damian Penner; Michael Zwaagstra; Jac Siemens
seconder: Jac Siemens; Susan Penner; Bill Hiebert; Bill Hiebert
vote: unanimous of those present (J. Hiebert absent Aug 1)
notes: Minutes list the subdivision as 4451-2023-8550 in R23-159 and 8850 in the hearing heading; same file.

title: 360-368 Third Street apartment rezoning denied after neighbourhood opposition
summary: Kingdom Home Building Inc. sought to rezone three Third Street lots from RLD to RMD for a three-storey apartment building (about 32 units, per an objector). A 40-plus-name petition and about a dozen neighbours objected (scale, character, traffic, problems at existing rentals, property values). Midway through the hearing the applicant asked to adjourn for two months to redesign and consult; council refused, saying consultation should happen before a hearing, and the applicant then asked to withdraw. Council denied second reading unanimously. Members said the site was outside the OCP transitional zone, which 'ends at 2nd Street'.
status_detail: Second reading of By-law 2231 denied Aug 1, 2023 (R23-160); first reading had passed Jul 4, 2023 (R23-139). Council had denied a similar rezoning of the same lots about 10-11 years earlier.
figures: Petition of 40-plus signatures (transcript 0:46:13); 13 objectors listed in the minutes; 4 letters of correspondence (City Manager, 0:23:46).
reasons: neighbours-object: Strong turnout and petition; 'public hearings do matter'; decision based on respect for the community. (Michael Zwaagstra; Bill Hiebert; Earl Funk); neighbourhood-not-ready: 'Leapfrogging': the OCP transitional zone ends at Second Street, not Third. (Damian Penner; Jac Siemens); study-first: Developer should consult neighbours and bring actual plans before the hearing, not table midway. (Michael Zwaagstra; Damian Penner)
public: Objectors (initials): L.A., P.P., T.B. (presented a 40-plus-name petition), G.F., K.P., S.P., N.V.G., M.R., S.A., T.L., G.R., A.G., K.V.G. Concerns: building too big and high for a single-family block, OCP infill compatibility, traffic, privacy, and police calls at the existing rentals on the lots (unproven allegations about specific tenants). The applicant (L.W., Kingdom Home Building Inc.) cited near-0% vacancy in its buildings and demand for downtown infill.
notes: Some public-speaker turns are mis-labelled in the transcript (several residents' names appear under the applicant's or mayor's label); only clearly attributed turns are quoted.

title: Development fees raised 5% a year for 2024-2027 (By-law 2233), not staff's recommended 7.5%
summary: Staff proposed combining the residential and non-residential capital development fee by-laws and the water and sewer impact fee by-law into one, with fees rising 7.5% a year for four years because the old 2.5% annual increases had fallen behind construction costs. Councillor Zwaagstra moved to amend the increase to 5%, matching construction inflation since 2012, to protect affordability. Councillors Damian Penner and Jake Hiebert voted against at every reading, arguing that existing taxpayers subsidize growth through the mill rate when fees lag. The by-law passed 5-2.
status_detail: Adopted 5-2 at all three readings (R23-211 Oct 17; R23-224, R23-225 Nov 7, 2023), but at 5% a year rather than staff's 7.5%; members agreed even 7.5% would not cover the cost of growth. Fees to be reviewed in 2027.
figures: Fees had risen 2.5% a year since 2012-2013 while construction inflation ran about 5-6% (Zwaagstra, Oct 17, 0:08:47); SPC options were 2.5%, 5%, 7.5% and 10%, with about 11% needed over four years to restore earlier cost coverage (D. Penner, Nov 7, 0:07:13). By-law 2233 schedule (city website, per the published report): $4,083 per single-family home in 2024 rising to $4,727 in 2027; $3,112 per apartment unit in 2025; water and sewer impact fees apply only to non-residential development.
reasons: fees-hurt-affordability: Every increase is passed on to buyers; prefers to 'err on the side of affordability' because the city needs more homes. (Michael Zwaagstra); fees-hurt-affordability: Entry-level housing would be hit hardest by 7.5%; other governments are trying to cut housing costs. (Earl Funk); fees-hurt-affordability: Would not have supported 7.5%; avoid pricing Steinbach out of the market. (Susan Penner); fees-hurt-affordability: Agreed with 7.5% in principle but 'too big an increase would hurt growth rate'; review in 2027. (Jac Siemens)
public: No public speakers; the by-law had no public hearing.
seconder: Jac Siemens; Bill Hiebert; Susan Penner
notes: At Nov 7, 2023 (0:06:24) a supporting comment ('This actually gives benefit to people that are looking at building') is mis-attributed to the City Manager in the speaker map; likely a councillor, not quoted. Exact 2024-2027 dollar schedule comes from the by-law on the city website as cited in the existing report, not re-checked against the package (no 2023 package on file).

title: 600 Main Street rezoned for a sixplex, with a lot-width variance
summary: Owners of 600 Main Street (residents, initials H.B. and I.B.) rezoned the lot from RLD to RMD for a six-unit building of two-bedroom apartments and got a variance for a 70-foot lot where 75 is required. One neighbour (P.K.) said a fourplex would fit better and asked for a fence to stop back-lane parking; another resident (H.W.) supported more density. Council approved unanimously without imposing the fence, preferring flexible mitigation.
status_detail: First reading Dec 19, 2023 (R23-259); second and third readings Jan 16, 2024 (R24-004, R24-005); variance V-2023-23 approved (R24-006).
figures: 6 two-bedroom units; lot 70 ft vs 75 ft minimum (transcript 0:08:26, 0:20:16).
public: P.K. (neighbour) preferred a fourplex and back-lane controls; H.W. supported more units given the housing crisis.
mover: Michael Zwaagstra; Susan Penner; Jac Siemens; Damian Penner
seconder: Susan Penner; Bill Hiebert; Michael Zwaagstra; Michael Zwaagstra

title: Record housing growth reported: 120 units in 2023, a record 2024 led by multi-family
summary: Monthly building-permit reports showed housing slowing in 2023 (120 dwelling units, a commercial-heavy year led by the hospital expansion) and then surging in 2024, with multi-family outpacing single- and two-family units. The mayor reported 1,533 housing units added 2015-2022 and $80.5M of infrastructure installed by the city and developers. Members credited supply for easing costs and said housing follows commercial growth.
status_detail: Permit reports accepted monthly. The published report cites 344 units permitted in 2024 (SteinbachOnline), the most on record.
figures: 2023: 120 dwelling units (D. Penner, Jan 16, 2024, 1:44:18). 2024 year to date: 43 by March, 151 by July, 174 by September (72 single/two-family, 102 multi-family per Oct 1, 2024 package p. 33), 267 by October (S. Penner, Nov 19, 2024). 2020: 302 units; 2021: 289 (Mayor, Dec 17, 2024). 2015-2022: 1,533 housing units and $80.5M infrastructure (Mayor, Sept 3, 2024).
reasons: market-decides: Supply growth is the best counter to rising costs. (Damian Penner)
notes: Permit counts are permits, not completions.

title: Park Hill (Kootenay Way): 22-lot subdivision and rezoning to medium density for multi-family
summary: Sincerus (Park Hill) GP Ltd. subdivided five lots into 22 north of McKenzie Avenue and rezoned one parcel from RLD to RMD for multi-family, adjusting its earlier plan to market demand. No one objected. Members praised the developer's flexibility to 'move to the market'.
status_detail: By-law 2236 first reading Feb 6 (R24-027); subdivision 4451-2024-8941 approved (R24-084) and By-law 2236 second and third readings (R24-085, R24-086) Apr 16, 2024, all unanimous.
figures: 5 lots into 22 lots, mix of two-family and multi-family (transcript 0:06:47, 0:09:02).
public: No objections.
mover: Damian Penner; Michael Zwaagstra; Susan Penner; Jake Hiebert
seconder: Michael Zwaagstra; Jac Siemens; Damian Penner; Michael Zwaagstra

title: 268/274 Home Street: 32-unit, three-storey apartment rezoning passes second reading 4-3 over a 43-name petition
themes: infill; rezoning; apartments; density; affordable-housing; parking
summary: Kingdom Home Building Inc. applied to rezone two single-family lots near Bethesda hospital and the event centre from RLD to RMD for a 32-unit, three-storey building with an elevator and partly underground parking (55 stalls vs 53 required). The hearing drew a 43-name petition and many neighbours who said the block is affordable entry-level ownership housing, not run down, and outside the transitional zone; several residents spoke in favour of downtown density. Council split 4-3: Susan Penner, Jac Siemens, Bill Hiebert and the mayor for (downtown vitality, hospital workers, seniors, growing up not out); Michael Zwaagstra, Jake Hiebert and Damian Penner against (neighbours' wishes, single-family homes are good too, not in the transitional zone). Objections sent the by-law to the Municipal Board (hearing Aug 14-16, 2024).
status_detail: First reading Feb 20, 2024 (R24-038); second reading 4-3 Mar 19, 2024 (R24-061); Municipal Board delegation Aug 6, 2024 (R24-159). A four-storey (parking) variance and further steps came in 2025, outside this period.
figures: 32 units, 3 storeys over parking, 55 stalls vs 53 required (applicant, 0:15:35); petition of 43 names and 8 items of correspondence (City Manager, 0:09:12); developer said its 6 lots at 55/71 First St went from $7,689 to $67,525 net annual tax after redevelopment (applicant claim, 0:17:06).
reasons: neighbours-object: Strong turnout from people who live there; council should weigh neighbours over outside speakers. (Michael Zwaagstra; Jake Hiebert; Damian Penner); neighbourhood-not-ready: Not in the OCP transitional zone; a well-kept area, not run down; a duplex or fourplex might suit better. (Michael Zwaagstra; Jake Hiebert); already-doing-enough: More housing is needed but is already being built in other parts of the city. (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: Against (initials): K.D., D.T., G.W., D.W., S.R., A.K., M.P. (organized the 43-name petition), J.B., L.P., E.D., A.T., E.W. Main points: loss of affordable entry-level homes for young families, traffic and parking near the hospital, privacy, construction fatigue from the hospital and event centre, mature trees, and that the developer did not reach them. For: G.S. (downtown vitality, walkability, taxes), J.W. (the applicant's father), H.W. (infill cheaper than sprawl), C.S. (renting is his only option and vacancy is near zero). The applicant (L.W., Kingdom Home Building Inc.) cited 0% vacancy at its Steinbach buildings for 12 months.
mover: Damian Penner (first reading); Susan Penner (second reading); Jake Hiebert (Municipal Board delegation)
seconder: Michael Zwaagstra; Jac Siemens; Michael Zwaagstra
vote: R24-061: 4-3 (for: Funk, Siemens, S. Penner, B. Hiebert; against: D. Penner, J. Hiebert, Zwaagstra)
notes: Seconds are the start of each speaker turn (the published report's links for some of these quotes point a little later within the same turn). B. Hiebert's 1:44:46 turn is medium-confidence in the map and is not quoted.

title: 330 First Street: 15-unit all-residential building allowed in a commercial zone (no ground-floor commercial)
summary: A developer (W.N., applicant for the owner Skyprom Marketing Inc.) could not find commercial tenants for a long-vacant C2 lot in the OCP's central business district transitional area, so council approved a conditional use for a 15-suite, three-storey residential building and a variance dropping the required main-floor commercial component. Two neighbours objected over privacy, noise, garbage and rental upkeep; one resident supported more multi-family near downtown.
status_detail: CU-2024-01 approved (R24-062) and V-2024-02 approved (R24-063), Mar 19, 2024, both unanimous, subject to a development agreement.
figures: 15 suites, 3 storeys; 126 ft from the nearest house to the back of the building; 25-ft green buffer (applicant, 1:56:33).
public: Against: R.B. (privacy, rental upkeep, building quality), E.B. (privacy, noise, lighting, garbage). For: S.J. (supports more multi-family near downtown but would prefer owned units to rentals).
notes: The proposed 2024 zoning changes (Dec 3, 2024) would permit stand-alone multi-unit residential in the transitional district, matching this approval.

title: 362/366 Main Street: six-storey mixed-use building (commercial below, apartments above) approved
summary: Council approved a conditional use for multi-family residential in the C2 zone and a height variance to six storeys and 78 feet (instead of five storeys and 50 feet) for a mixed-use building on vacant Main Street lots, with parking at the back. Every member praised it as the long-held vision for a denser downtown; the mayor noted the city had to wait for a developer to act.
status_detail: CU-2024-04 (R24-116) and V-2024-04 (R24-117) approved unanimously Jun 18, 2024, subject to a development agreement.
figures: 6 storeys, 78 ft vs 5 storeys / 50 ft allowed (City Manager, 0:24:12).
reasons: market-decides: Downtown density is 'developer-driven'; council had to wait for a developer. (Earl Funk)
public: One item of correspondence; no objector spoke.

title: Council backs enforcement of basement-suite safety rules despite fears of losing low-cost rentals
summary: The 2021 Dwelling Unit Safety Standards By-law 2157 set basic life-safety rules (smoke and CO alarms, egress) for rental and secondary suites instead of full building-code compliance, to avoid decommissioning many suites. With only a few dozen of an estimated several hundred suites voluntarily compliant and several recent house fires, staff proposed direct outreach, work orders and fines up to $1,000 a day. All members supported it; Councillor Siemens said council had held off for fear of losing many low-end rental units, and the mayor said the fixes are small costs.
status_detail: Council gave consensus support Aug 20, 2024 (recorded in the minutes without a resolution number); administration began proactive enforcement immediately.
figures: Up to several hundred secondary suites estimated; only several dozen voluntarily compliant; maximum fine $1,000 per day (transcript 0:13:28, 0:17:25).
reasons: lose-low-cost-rentals: Why council held off enforcing: it could remove many low-end rental units when rentals are already scarce. (Jac Siemens)
notes: Jake Hiebert's turn is from a merged speaker cluster (medium) and is paraphrased, not quoted.

title: Kingdom Home Building's First Street proposals: 6-storey, 100-unit high-density rezoning and a 40 First Street apartment rezoning
summary: Council gave first reading to two rezonings by Kingdom Home Building Inc. near First and Giesbrecht streets: By-law 2252 (RLD to RHD for a six-storey, 100-unit complex, which members called among the largest housing proposals they had seen) and By-law 2253 (RLD to RMD at 40 First Street for a building with ground-level parking and two residential floors). At the Nov 5, 2024 hearing on 2253 two neighbours asked about the design, demolition, green space, traffic and drainage; council gave second reading unanimously.
status_detail: By-law 2252: first reading Oct 1, 2024 (R24-191); no hearing found in the record by Dec 2024. By-law 2253: first reading Oct 1 (R24-192), second reading Nov 5, 2024 (R24-207); third reading came Feb 17, 2026 (R26-044).
figures: By-law 2252: 6 storeys, 100 units (Zwaagstra, Oct 1, 0:09:20). 40 First St lot 72 ft wide vs 75 ft RMD minimum, minor variance by administration (minutes Nov 5, 2024).
public: At the Nov 5, 2024 hearing (minutes only): E.B. (owner of a neighbouring property) asked whether the drawing is what will be built and about green space; G.W. raised traffic and drainage. The applicant (L.W., Kingdom Home Building Inc.) said the site is walkable to downtown.
mover: Michael Zwaagstra; Jac Siemens; Susan Penner
seconder: Damian Penner; Susan Penner; Michael Zwaagstra
notes: Zwaagstra's Oct 1 remarks are medium-confidence in the speaker map and are used only for figures. The Nov 5, 2024 meeting has no recording.

title: OCP and zoning by-law review: affordable-housing policies, one-third less downtown parking, detached suites in rural zones
themes: affordable-housing; secondary-suites; parking; density; process; supportive-housing
summary: After a review begun in 2023, council accepted administration's recommended changes for a new Official Community Plan and zoning by-law and authorized drafting: new OCP policies on affordable housing and on keeping and creating rental units; parking reduced by one-third for all uses in the central business district ('council has approved virtually every variance for reduced parking'); stand-alone multi-unit residential and mixed-use dwellings allowed more freely downtown and in the transitional district; detached secondary suites as a conditional use only in rural and development-reserve zones (owner-occupied); and a new 'emergency residential shelter' definition made a conditional use so neighbours get a hearing.
status_detail: Direction approved Dec 3, 2024 (R24-234); public engagement planned for January 2025 and first readings for February 2025 (outside this period). The published report notes the zoning by-law adopted in 2026 kept 1.5 stalls per apartment and no 3-4 units per lot.
figures: Zoning by-law cut from 155 to 106 pages (City Manager, 0:06:35). Package summary: affordable-housing policies 4.1.17-4.1.18; 'The city should adopt tools and programs to maximize the creation and retention of a wide range of housing, and the retention and creation of rental units (4.1.2.17)'; detached secondary suites conditional in DR1, DR2, RR-S, RR; emergency residential shelter conditional in R-MX, C1-C4, C-MX, EI (Dec 3, 2024 package, pp. 10-14).
public: Public engagement scheduled after this meeting.
notes: At 0:12:51 the speaker map labels the City Planner's remarks as Susan Penner (same label E); only E turns after the Deputy Mayor names Councillor Penner are used.

title: City objects to RM of Hanover rezoning on its northern edge to protect land for future urban growth
summary: Council filed a formal objection to RM of Hanover By-law 2578-24, which would rezone a parcel just north of the city on PTH 12 after Hanover had approved a subdivision and issued building permits. Members said it broke Hanover's development plan, provincial policy and the Steinbach-Hanover annexation agreement, and would fragment land the city needs to grow into.
status_detail: Objection authorized Dec 17, 2024 (R24-246); Hanover's hearing was set for Jan 8, 2025 (outcome not in this record).
notes: The disputed development is commercial/industrial, not housing; included because it concerns land for future urban (including residential) growth.

title: Record housing permits in 2024 and 2025, most of them apartments
summary: Each month council accepts the building-permit report, and members used it to track a housing boom: a record 344 dwelling units in 2024, a new record of 365 in 2025, and 148 units in August 2026 alone. Members said most new homes are now multi-family and that rental vacancy remains very low.
status_detail: Permit reports accepted unanimously every month. Permits are not completions. By the end of September 2026 the city had 303 housing starts for the year (mayor, Oct 20, 2026).
figures: 344 dwelling units in 2024 (S. Penner, Jan 21, 2025 0:26:16); 365 in 2025 (mayor, Jan 20, 2026 0:31:51); 72 units in March 2025 (Apr 15, 2025); 148 units in August 2026, a monthly record (S. Penner, Sep 15, 2026 0:52:16); 303 housing starts to end of Sept 2026 (mayor, Oct 20, 2026 0:16:53); last 3 years: 253 single-family/duplex and 755 multi-family units, about 75% multi-family (B. Hiebert, Sep 15, 2026 0:00:00)
notes: Unit counts are building-permit counts as read out at council, not CMHC completions.

title: 17 homes approved at 79/85 First Street (By-law 2260)
summary: Vogt Building Construction asked to rezone two First Street lots from low to medium density for a 17-unit, story-and-a-half building with 2- and 3-bedroom units. No one objected and no variances were needed; council approved all three readings unanimously.
status_detail: Third reading given May 6, 2025 (R25-100), subject to a development agreement.
figures: 17 units; 122 new residential units created in the First Street area since 2018 (D. Penner, Jan 21, 2025 0:12:47)
public: No objectors at the Feb 18, 2025 hearing; the province had no concerns.

title: Lift Station 1, second force main and sewer mains built for growth
summary: Council approved Local Improvement Plan 2025-01 to twin the 3-km force main from Lift Station 1 to the lagoon, asked the Manitoba Water Services Board for 50% of the cost, and in 2026 awarded contracts for Lift Station 1 upgrades, the Park Road West force main and a Millwork Drive sewer main. Members said the system was near capacity because of housing growth.
status_detail: By-law 2255 third reading Jul 2, 2025 (R25-137); contracts awarded Feb 17, 2026 (R26-038), Mar 3, 2026 (R26-050) and Mar 17, 2026 (R26-060).
figures: Force main $6.595M, up to $2.75M borrowed over 5 years (Warkentin, Feb 4, 2025 0:05:25); generator $670,600 (R25-210); Park Road West forcemain $1,494,661.05 (R26-038); Millwork Drive sewer $1,462,540 (R26-050); Lift Station 1 upgrades $4,326,078.39, capacity 482 to 843 L/s (R26-060; Zwaagstra, Mar 17, 2026 1:54:37)
public: Georgetown residents (M.R. and others) linked repeated sewer backups to new subdivisions and apartments added to an old line; covered in the sewer-backups report.
notes: Bill Hiebert said on Feb 4, 2025 that the system was "almost at capacity" because of housing growth, but that speaker label is medium confidence, so he is not quoted.

title: Sixplex at 189 Hanover Street denied ("10 years too early")
summary: A young couple applied to rezone a vacant Hanover Street lot for a 6-unit building with no variances. Staff recommended approval subject to a development agreement. Several neighbours objected; council unanimously denied it, saying the mid-block, all-single-family location was not yet ready for apartments.
status_detail: By-law 2261 denied at second reading Mar 18, 2025 (R25-056).
figures: 6 units on a roughly half-acre lot (Siemens 0:36:35); 8 items of correspondence (Warkentin 0:08:20)
reasons: neighbourhood-not-ready: Area should transition later, after the commercial side of Hanover develops; duplex or fourplex would fit now (Jac Siemens); neighbours-object: Mid-block among single-family homes; does not fit neighbourhood character; listen to neighbours (Michael Zwaagstra); market-decides: Council is not driving density; projects are owner-driven and decided case by case (Mayor Earl Funk)
public: C.S., G.B. and other neighbours objected (traffic, parking, privacy, property values); J.W. doubted the traffic claims; the applicants (B.T., T.R.) cited high housing demand.
notes: Staff recommendation was second reading subject to a development agreement and the infill policy (Warkentin 0:08:20).

title: Fourth storey (parking level) allowed for 32-unit Home Street building, 3-2
summary: After the 2024 rezoning of 268/274 Home Street (approved 4-3, then upheld after a Municipal Board hearing), the builder asked for a fourth storey made of partly underground parking. Two neighbours objected. Council approved it 3-2 on condition the parking level sit no more than 1 metre above grade; Zwaagstra and J. Hiebert voted against, saying it allowed more units than a redesign would.
status_detail: Variance V-2025-02 approved with the 1-metre condition and a development agreement (R25-049). B. Hiebert and Siemens were excused.
figures: 4 storeys incl. a parking level no more than 1 m above grade (R25-049); rezoning itself was approved 4-3 in 2024 (Zwaagstra, 1:28:02)
reasons: neighbours-object: Many neighbours had objected to the rezoning; he would not support adding to it (Jake Hiebert); neighbourhood-not-ready: Opposed the original density; a denial would force a redesign with fewer units and less impact (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: W.K. and D.K. (Home Street) objected: loss of privacy and sunlight, tree removal, and construction fatigue near the hospital and event centre.

title: 2025 budget: 'growth pays for itself is not true'
summary: Moving the 2025 financial plan, Zwaagstra listed growth-driven borrowing (Loewen Blvd/PTH 12 intersection, water capacity, event centre, RCMP) and said growth does not pay for itself. The plan kept the mill rate and took on about $10 million in net new debt. No change to development fees was proposed in this period.
status_detail: Financial plan approved in principle Mar 4 (R25-048) and adopted Apr 15, 2025 (R25-082). Development fees remained as set by By-law 2233 (2024–2027); no fee debate occurred in 2025–26.
figures: $13.25M new debt vs $2.6M retired; Force Main borrowing $2.75M; property value growth 14.9% (Zwaagstra, Mar 4, 2025 0:31:04)
reasons: infrastructure-capacity: Growth forces spending on roads, water and sewer capacity, policing and facilities (Michael Zwaagstra)
notes: Development charges (By-law 2233) expire after 2027; no review was discussed in 2025–26 meetings.

title: No city affordable-housing program, incentive or federal housing application
summary: Across 2025–26 council did not create incentives, grants, fee waivers or land offers for affordable housing, did not commission a housing needs assessment, and no Housing Accelerator Fund application came to council. The mayor described affordable housing and homelessness as provincial responsibilities being downloaded to municipalities; members credited developers with supply.
status_detail: Nothing proposed or decided. Affordable units came from private projects (studios), non-profits (Steinbach Housing, Bridgepark) and endorsements (The Bridge on Third).
reasons: other-governments-fund: Affordable housing is 'usually in the province's basket'; wary of downloaded costs (Mayor Earl Funk); market-decides: Developers, not council, are driving new homes (Damian Penner)
notes: Searched all 2025–Nov 2026 transcripts for accelerator, CMHC, Manitoba Housing, needs assessment, incentive and development-fee terms; no such item found.

title: Sixplex approved at 286 Henry Street
summary: Rezoning of a corner lot at Loewen Blvd and Henry Street for a 6-unit building, with a narrower site width. Council approved the width variance but denied the reduced corner side yard, then gave the rezoning second and third readings unanimously.
status_detail: V-2025-07 approved in part (site width 64.5 ft yes; 4-ft corner side yard no) (R25-093); By-law 2262 passed (R25-094, R25-095). A 12-unit building next door followed in 2026 (see 2026-288-henry-street).
figures: 6 units; site width 64.5 ft vs 75 ft required (Warkentin, May 6, 2025 0:08:04)
reasons: infrastructure-capacity: Kept the 8-ft corner setback in case Loewen Blvd is ever widened (Jac Siemens)
public: C.M., a neighbour, did not oppose ("We need housing") but complained about upkeep of the rental property.

title: New Official Community Plan and Zoning By-law 2245 adopted
summary: After a joint public hearing on Apr 1, 2025, council gave first and second readings to the new OCP (By-law 2244) and Zoning By-law 2245. Changes included detached secondary suites (conditional use, rural residential only, owner on site), a one-third cut in required parking in the central business district, dropping the main-floor commercial expectation, and making emergency residential shelters a conditional use. Objections sent the zoning by-law to the Municipal Board, which ordered no changes.
status_detail: OCP third reading Sep 16, 2025 (R25-184) after minister approval without amendment; Zoning By-law 2245 third reading Jan 20, 2026 (R26-015) after the Municipal Board ruling.
figures: Zoning by-law cut from 155 to 106 pages (Apr 1, 2025 2:00:15, merged staff/councillor speaker label); CBD parking reduced by 1/3 (S. Penner 1:55:03; Zwaagstra Jan 20, 2026 0:29:47)
reasons: neighbours-object: Shelters/transitional housing should be conditional so neighbourhoods get a hearing, same as any residential in commercial zones (Susan Penner); study-first: Detached suites limited to rural residential, owner-occupied, conditional use (Susan Penner)
public: Many residents and The Inn board (a proposed transitional-housing project) spoke mainly about shelters being made a conditional use; L.C. raised Charter rulings on encampments. The hearing is covered in more detail in the homelessness report.
resolution_no: OCP: R25-069, R25-070, R25-184; Zoning: R25-071, R25-072, R25-181 (Municipal Board delegation), R26-015
mover: OCP 3rd: Susan Penner; Zoning 1st: Susan Penner; Zoning 3rd: Michael Zwaagstra
seconder: OCP 3rd: Michael Zwaagstra; Zoning 1st: Damian Penner; Zoning 3rd: Jake Hiebert
notes: Detached suites are limited to the RR rural residential zone (Warkentin, Apr 21, 2026 0:19:30). Per the existing report, By-law 2245 keeps 1.5 stalls per apartment unit plus visitor parking outside the CBD and does not allow 3–4 units per lot as of right; not re-checked against the by-law text here. The Apr 1, 2025 speaker cited for the 155→106 page figure is a merged label (staff/Zwaagstra), so it is not quoted.

title: Federal help sought for $132M wastewater treatment expansion
summary: Council ratified an application to the Canada Housing Infrastructure Fund for 50% of a roughly $132 million wastewater treatment expansion, lift station upgrades and a second force main, after choosing a city-only plant over joining the Red-Seine-Rat co-op (25–30% costlier). Members said the goal is never to have to stop issuing building permits, as Morden did.
status_detail: Application ratified (R25-081). No funding decision was reported at council through Nov 3, 2026. In May 2026 S. Penner said projected costs had risen to over $200 million.
figures: ~$132M project, 50% requested from CHIF (Zwaagstra, Apr 15, 2025 0:14:06); co-op option 25–30% more (Warkentin 0:15:25); "over $200 million" (S. Penner, May 5, 2026 0:00:12)
reasons: other-governments-fund: Project is unaffordable without substantial federal/provincial support (Michael Zwaagstra)
notes: S. Penner's May 5, 2026 opening calls it the 'new water treatment facility'; context suggests the wastewater plant but this is not confirmed. No charge on new homes for wastewater was discussed.

title: Subdivision of an apartment site on Woodhaven Ave denied
summary: Stone Creek Estates asked to split a high-density site at 236 Woodhaven Ave (two existing 3-storey buildings) into five lots, with access and services by easement, mainly for financing reasons. Staff raised policy concerns; council unanimously denied it as a bad precedent.
status_detail: Subdivision 4451-2024-9057 denied (R25-109). Development of further buildings on the single parcel was still possible.
figures: 5 lots from one RHD parcel; 2 existing 3-storey buildings (Warkentin, May 20, 2025 0:11:17)
reasons: fairness-precedent: Precedent-setting; not council's job to change policy to help a developer's financing (Damian Penner); fairness-precedent: Lots without direct road access create future disputes; financing should not override planning (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: The applicant's representatives argued subdivision would speed financing and development.
notes: Siemens spoke but his label is merged with a delegate (medium), so he is not quoted.

title: City objects to La Broquerie plan allowing rural duplexes near the boundary
summary: Council objected to RM of La Broquerie plan and zoning changes that would remove the transitional policy area within 2 miles of Steinbach and allow denser, rurally serviced development (including 2-unit dwellings) at the border, saying it would block future annexation and urban servicing. Earlier, staff were sent to a Municipal Board hearing on an RM of Hanover rezoning (Aug 2025).
status_detail: Objection R26-192 filed Sep 15, 2026; outcome not reported. Aug 19, 2025: R25-163 delegated the city manager and planner to the Municipal Board hearing on RM of Hanover By-law 2578-24 (minutes only; no recording; outcome not found).
figures: Transitional area = within 2 miles of the city (Sep 15, 2026 0:47:43, merged speaker label, read from staff report)
reasons: infrastructure-capacity: Rural development at the edge would block annexation and urban growth (Bill Hiebert)
notes: D. Penner's remarks on Sep 15, 2026 are on a medium-confidence label and are paraphrased only.

title: Duplex front-yard variance in a new subdivision passes 4-3
summary: Three Way Builders asked to build a duplex on a corner lot with a 17-ft front yard instead of 25 ft. The city engineer recommended denial over stormwater and precedent; the city manager recommended approval. Council split 4-3 a week after the September 2025 flooding.
status_detail: Variance V-2025-22 approved (R25-177).
figures: 17 ft vs 25 ft required front yard (Warkentin, Sep 16, 2025 0:07:11)
reasons: infrastructure-capacity: Larger footprint adds stormwater runoff; sets a precedent in a new subdivision (Michael Zwaagstra); fairness-precedent: Sided with the engineer's report on impermeable area (Mayor Earl Funk)
vote: 4-3 (against: Earl Funk, Jake Hiebert, Michael Zwaagstra)
notes: In this transcript one label (C) merges the city manager with at least two councillors, so councillors other than Zwaagstra and the mayor are not quoted; how each voted comes from the minutes.

title: Council backs call to raise provincial water/sewer grants to $100M
summary: Council endorsed a Manitoba Municipal Administrators resolution asking the province to raise the Manitoba Water Services Board capital budget from $24M to $100M a year, arguing growing towns cannot keep building homes without water and sewer capacity.
status_detail: Resolution R25-193 passed and sent; no provincial response reported at council.
figures: $24M/yr fund vs $1.35B requested; 103 municipalities with unfunded projects (mayor, Oct 7, 2025 0:26:10, 0:28:55); city project ~$130M (S. Penner 0:30:40)
reasons: other-governments-fund: Smaller cities cannot afford projects of this size alone (Susan Penner)

title: 36 studio apartments on Main Street with reduced parking (5-2)
summary: Hillside Custom proposed a 2-storey building of 36 studio units under 500 sq ft at 635/641 Main St, aiming for rents under $1,000, with 45 parking stalls instead of the 59 required. Council rezoned the land unanimously and approved the parking variance 5-2, calling it a test of a new affordable model.
status_detail: By-law 2266 second reading Nov 18, 2025 (R25-221) and third reading Jan 20, 2026 (R26-012); Variance V-2025-32 approved Nov 18, 2025 (R25-222).
figures: 36 units under 500 sq ft; 45 stalls vs 59 required (Warkentin, Nov 18, 2025 0:17:32; S. Penner 0:45:29); applicant target rent below $1,000/month (0:37:57)
reasons: parking-rules: Most residents will own at least one car; no evidence of fewer visitors (Michael Zwaagstra); fairness-precedent: A 24% parking cut sets a lasting precedent; another floor would have solved parking (Jake Hiebert)
public: No neighbours objected. The applicant's representative (T.T.) said lower height and smaller units were chosen to keep rent attractive.
seconder: Damian Penner (1st, 3rd); Bill Hiebert (2nd); Jac Siemens (variance)
vote: rezoning unanimous; variance 5-2 (against: Jake Hiebert, Michael Zwaagstra)

title: Park Hill Phase 2C: 41 lots, rezoned toward duplexes and townhouses
summary: Sincerus (Park Hill) subdivided land north of McKenzie Ave into 41 lots and rezoned them from single-family to low and medium density to match demand. One letter objected because sidewalks would not be built on every street; staff said sidewalks are deliberately not required from developers and are added later by the city. Approved unanimously.
status_detail: Subdivision 4451-2025-9173 approved (R25-245); By-law 2268 second and third readings (R25-246, R25-247). Phase 2C street lighting added Feb 3, 2026 (R26-032).
figures: 41 lots: lots 1–9, 21, 22 to RLD; lots 23–41 to RMD (Warkentin, Dec 16, 2025 0:09:33)
reasons: market-decides: Developers know best where housing demand is; council should be flexible (Susan Penner)
public: One written conditional objection asked for sidewalks on all listed streets.
mover: Michael Zwaagstra (subdivision); Susan Penner (2nd); Jake Hiebert (3rd)
seconder: Susan Penner (subdivision); Bill Hiebert (2nd); Michael Zwaagstra (3rd)
notes: The minutes record first reading of a rezoning on Nov 18, 2025 as "By-Law 2286" (R25-225); the transcript shows this was By-law 2268 (Park Hill 2C). Likely a typo in the minutes.

title: 31 apartments in a 5-storey and a 3-storey building on First Street
summary: Neustaedter Holdings got conditional use to build apartments in a C-1 zone on First Street (two buildings, 19 and 12 units) and variances to drop the main-floor commercial requirement and allow 5 storeys. Neighbours asked about parking, stormwater and traffic. Approved unanimously.
status_detail: CU-2025-05 (R25-248) and V-2025-35 (R25-249) approved subject to a development agreement. A related lot realignment was approved Sep 15, 2026 (R26-196).
figures: 2 buildings, 19 and 12 units; 5 storeys incl. main-floor parking (J. Hiebert, Dec 16, 2025 0:40:22; applicant 0:22:37)
public: R.P. and J.G. (First Street) asked about unit numbers, parking (2 vehicles per unit vs 1.5 required), stormwater and traffic.

title: 33-unit mixed-use building at 31 Loewen Blvd; later more homes, less commercial
summary: Council allowed a 4-storey mixed-use building (33 apartments over 10,000 sq ft of commercial) at 31 Loewen Blvd in January 2026. In October 2026 the builder, unable to lease the commercial space, was allowed to put residential units on most of the main floor. J. Hiebert worried it was becoming an apartment block in a commercial corridor.
status_detail: CU-2025-06 (R26-003) and V-2025-38 (R26-004) approved Jan 6, 2026; Variance V-2026-21 carried Oct 20, 2026 (transcript; minutes not yet available).
figures: 33 units + 10,000 sq ft commercial (Warkentin, Jan 6, 2026 0:13:31); Oct 2026: 9 main-floor residential units added, one ~1,800–1,900 sq ft commercial space (J. Hiebert and applicant, Oct 20, 2026)
reasons: market-decides: Developers know what the market wants; commercial is hard to lease (Mayor Earl Funk)
public: No objectors. The applicant's representative (N.T.) said commercial tenants would not wait for construction.
resolution_no: R26-003, R26-004; Oct 20, 2026 not yet in minutes
mover: Damian Penner (CU); Michael Zwaagstra (variance); Susan Penner (Oct 20)
seconder: Michael Zwaagstra (CU); Bill Hiebert (variance); "Councilor Bill Pinner" (Oct 20, as transcribed)
vote: unanimous (Jan); Oct 20 carried, no recorded dissent heard

title: Routine approvals that opened more sites for apartments
summary: Grouped uncontested items: third reading for a 3-storey building over open parking at First St/Giesbrecht (By-law 2253); renewal of a 2022 residential subdivision approval held up by Manning Canal talks; subdivisions to create multi-unit sites at 60 McKenzie, 190–206 First St and 6 Langille Way; and a variance letting a high-density Park Hill lot be built out at 3 storeys.
status_detail: All approved unanimously.
public: At 100 Kootenay Way a neighbour (E.H.) asked to move garbage bins; no other objections.
mover: Jac Siemens (R26-030, R26-044); Jake Hiebert (R26-113, R26-196, R26-204); Susan Penner (R26-202)
seconder: Jake Hiebert (R26-030); Susan Penner (R26-044); Bill Hiebert (R26-113, R26-196); Michael Zwaagstra (R26-202); Damian Penner (R26-204)

title: 48 apartments on McKenzie Ave approved despite petition
summary: Three lots at 492–506 McKenzie Ave were rezoned for 48 units in 3-storey buildings with no variances. A petition and several neighbours objected (traffic, drainage, sewer backups, privacy, a 2-storey character); one neighbour already living beside a new 3-storey building spoke in favour. Council approved it unanimously, citing a collector street near Highway 52, nil vacancy and no parking variance.
status_detail: By-law 2273 second reading Apr 7, 2026 (R26-068), third reading Sep 1, 2026 (R26-184), subject to a development agreement.
figures: 48 units, 3 storeys, 1.5 stalls per unit, no variances (Warkentin, Apr 7, 2026 0:06:46; Zwaagstra 1:22:56)
public: H.K. presented a petition and asked council to deny; A.R., C.V.B., J.D., P.K. and B.D. (for a neighbouring church) raised drainage, sewer, traffic and privacy concerns. G.S., who lives beside a new 3-storey building, supported it: the city needs density to pay its bills.
mover: Michael Zwaagstra (1st); Damian Penner (2nd); Jake Hiebert (3rd)

title: 7-storey, ~84-unit affordable seniors building with 1:1 parking (5-2)
summary: Steinbach Housing proposed a 7-storey building of about 84 one-bedroom seniors' apartments at 185 Friesen Ave beside Linden Place. The first proposal (91 units, 10 stalls instead of 150) was adjourned in March to get a parking plan. In June council allowed multi-family use unanimously and approved the height and one stall per unit (139 required) 5-2. Zwaagstra's amendment to keep the height but deny the parking cut found no seconder.
status_detail: Hearing adjourned Mar 17, 2026 to get a parking plan (R26-059, 6-1, Siemens against: ready to decide). CU-2026-03 (R26-109) and V-2026-05 (R26-110) approved Jun 2, 2026, subject to a development agreement. The Jun 2 minutes do not record a decision on the 1989 caveat reserving green space.
figures: ~84 units (applicant, Jun 2, 2026 0:09:53); 139 stalls required at 1.5/unit + 10% (Warkentin 0:11:49); first proposal 7 storeys, 10 stalls vs 150 required (Warkentin, Mar 17, 2026 0:50:40)
reasons: parking-rules: Street parking already full; 139 stalls is simply what the by-law requires (Michael Zwaagstra); parking-rules: Parking is a big issue; go with the by-law (Bill Hiebert); neighbourhood-not-ready: In March: honour the 1989 green-space agreement; C-1 allows 3 storeys, not 7 (he later voted for) (Jac Siemens)
public: R.L., speaking for several Friesen Ave households, objected to the height, loss of green space set aside in 1989, and parking, while saying neighbours want seniors housed.
seconder: Jake Hiebert (adjournment); Susan Penner (CU); Jac Siemens (variance)
vote: adjournment 6-1 (against: Jac Siemens); CU unanimous; variance 5-2 (against: Michael Zwaagstra, Bill Hiebert)

title: First detached secondary suite approved under the new by-law
summary: Council approved the first detached secondary ("granny") suite under Zoning By-law 2245, converting an existing building on a 2-acre rural residential lot at 840 Main St. Members framed suites as a way to keep families together.
status_detail: CU-2026-04 approved subject to a development agreement (R26-079). Detached suites remain limited to the RR zone.
figures: 2-acre lot (S. Penner, Apr 21, 2026 0:22:07)
public: No objections.

title: Transitional housing added to the zoning by-law, as a conditional use only
summary: The Inn (applicant L.C.) asked council to define transitional housing and make it a permitted use in the C-2 zone. Council defined it (3 months to 3 years, with supports) but made it a conditional use in seven zones, so every project needs a public hearing, with 1 parking space per 5 units or beds.
status_detail: By-law 2275 passed (R26-084, R26-111, R26-112) as a conditional use, not the permitted use requested. No transitional-housing project had come forward by Nov 2026.
figures: Conditional in RMD, RHD, RMX, C1, C2, C3, CMX; parking 1 space per 5 units/beds (Warkentin, Apr 21, 2026 0:45:53; Jun 2, 2026 1:05:59)
reasons: neighbours-object: Neighbourhoods must get a say on projects that may change their character (Susan Penner); neighbours-object: Could change the character of a neighbourhood, so a public hearing makes sense (Michael Zwaagstra)
public: The Inn sought a permitted use; no one spoke at the June 2 hearing.
mover: Susan Penner (1st); Michael Zwaagstra (2nd); Jac Siemens (3rd)
seconder: Michael Zwaagstra (1st); Damian Penner (2nd); Jake Hiebert (3rd)

title: Council endorses The Bridge on Third supportive housing (no city funds)
